notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: In what sense are finite-variance random variables "vectors"? Give the inner product, the norm, and what orthogonality means.
notes.back:
They form the Hilbert space \(L^2\) with inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle = E[XY]\).
For centered variables: \(\|X\|^2 = \mathrm{Var}(X)\), so length = standard deviation, \(\langle X,Y\rangle = \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)\), and orthogonal = uncorrelated.
notes.extra: Geometry: Every second-moment fact in statistics is Euclidean geometry in this space: lengths are standard deviations, angles are correlations, "best predictor" means "orthogonal projection". Most of regression is Pythagoras in disguise.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: What is the geometric meaning of the Pearson correlation \(\rho(X,Y)\)?
notes.back: \(\rho = \dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y} = \dfrac{\langle X,Y\rangle}{\|X\|\,\|Y\|} = \cos\theta\), the cosine of the angle between the centered variables (or, in a sample, between the centered data vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\rho=1\): parallel. \(\rho=0\): perpendicular. \(\rho=-1\): anti-parallel. This is why \(|\rho|\le 1\) is just Cauchy-Schwarz, and why correlation is not transitive: A can be at 45° to B and B at 45° to C while A is at 90° to C.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: State \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)\) and identify the geometric theorem it corresponds to.
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)\).
It is the law of cosines: \(\|x+y\|^2 = \|x\|^2+\|y\|^2+2\|x\|\|y\|\cos\theta\). When uncorrelated (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)) it reduces to Pythagoras.
notes.extra: Geometry: Standard deviations add like sides of a triangle, not like numbers. Independent errors add at right angles, which is why the standard error of a mean shrinks as \(1/\sqrt{n}\): the diagonal of an n-dimensional box with side \(\sigma\) is \(\sigma\sqrt{n}\), then divide by n.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: What is the conditional expectation \(E[Y\mid X]\) geometrically?
notes.back: The orthogonal projection of \(Y\) onto the closed subspace of all (square-integrable) functions of \(X\). Equivalently it minimises \(E[(Y-g(X))^2]\) over all \(g\), and the error \(Y - E[Y\mid X]\) is orthogonal to every function of \(X\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Linear regression projects onto the small subspace spanned by linear functions of \(X\); conditional expectation projects onto the much larger subspace of all functions of \(X\). The tower property \(E[E[Y|X,Z]\,|\,X]=E[Y|X]\) is just "projecting onto a subspace of a subspace in two steps equals projecting once".

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: State the law of total variance and its geometric interpretation.
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathrm{Var}(E[Y\mid X]) + E[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]\)
= explained variance + unexplained variance.
notes.extra: Geometry: Pythagoras. \(Y - E[Y]\) is the hypotenuse; the projection \(E[Y|X]-E[Y]\) and the residual \(Y-E[Y|X]\) are the perpendicular legs. \(R^2\) and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) are both this single right triangle.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: What shape does a covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) describe, and what do its eigenvectors and eigenvalues mean?
notes.back: The level sets \(x^\top\Sigma^{-1}x = c\) are ellipsoids. Eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) are the principal axes; the semi-axis lengths are \(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\) (standard deviations along those axes). \(\det\Sigma\) is proportional to the squared volume.
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) is the linear map that turns the unit sphere (white noise) into this ellipsoid. Every multivariate Gaussian is a rotated, stretched, shifted spherical Gaussian.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Define the Mahalanobis distance and explain what it measures.
notes.back:
\(d_M(x,\mu) = \sqrt{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}\).
It is the Euclidean distance after whitening the data with \(z = \Sigma^{-1/2}(x-\mu)\): distance measured in units of standard deviation along each principal axis.
notes.extra: Geometry: Squash the covariance ellipsoid back into a unit sphere, then use an ordinary ruler. A point far away along a long axis of the ellipse is less surprising than a point the same Euclidean distance away along a short axis.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: For a joint Gaussian \((x_1,x_2)\), give the conditional distribution \(x_1\mid x_2\). What is remarkable about the conditional covariance?
notes.back:
\(E[x_1\mid x_2] = \mu_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2-\mu_2)\)
\(\mathrm{Cov}[x_1\mid x_2] = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\) (the Schur complement).
The mean is linear in \(x_2\) (this is exactly the regression formula) and the covariance does not depend on the observed value.
notes.extra: Geometry: Conditioning = slicing the ellipsoid with a plane \(x_2 = \text{const}\). Every parallel slice of an ellipsoid is the same ellipse shape, just shifted along a straight line: hence constant covariance and linear mean.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Geometrically, how do marginalising and conditioning a multivariate Gaussian differ?
notes.back:
Marginalising = projecting (casting a shadow): just drop rows/columns of \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\).
Conditioning = slicing: simple in the precision matrix \(\Lambda=\Sigma^{-1}\) (drop rows/columns of \(\Lambda\)), but needs a Schur complement in \(\Sigma\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Shadow of an ellipsoid is wider than any slice through it. Hence marginal variance \(\ge\) conditional variance. Covariance is the natural language of shadows, precision is the natural language of slices. Zeros in \(\Sigma\) mean marginal independence; zeros in \(\Lambda\) mean conditional independence (graphical models).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: State the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and give an intuition for why the Gaussian is the limit.
notes.back:
For independent, identically distributed variables with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\): \(\sqrt{n}(\bar X_n-\mu) \xrightarrow{d} N(0,\sigma^2)\).
Why Gaussian: adding independent variables convolves densities; the Gaussian is the fixed point of "convolve and rescale", and it is the maximum-entropy distribution for a given variance, so repeated mixing that preserves only variance ends there.
notes.extra: Geometry: Convolution is repeated blurring. Blur any shape often enough and all detail except location and width is erased, leaving the blur kernel's universal shape. In Fourier space: the characteristic function near 0 is \(1 - \sigma^2t^2/2\); raising it to the n-th power gives \(e^{-\sigma^2 t^2/2}\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Why does a sample variance divide by \(n-1\)? Answer geometrically.
notes.back: The residual vector \(x - \bar x\mathbf{1}\) is the projection of \(x\) onto the hyperplane orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}=(1,\dots,1)\). That hyperplane has dimension \(n-1\), so the noise only has \(n-1\) free coordinates: \(E\|x-\bar x\mathbf{1}\|^2 = (n-1)\sigma^2\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Degrees of freedom = dimension of the subspace the vector lives in. Isotropic noise puts \(\sigma^2\) of expected squared length into each dimension. Fitting p parameters removes p dimensions from the residual, leaving \(n-p\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: What is the \(\chi^2_k\) distribution geometrically, and why does it appear everywhere in testing?
notes.back:
It is the distribution of the squared length of a standard Gaussian vector in \(k\) dimensions: \(\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i^2\). Mean \(k\), variance \(2k\).
It appears because test statistics are squared lengths of projections of (approximately) Gaussian noise onto subspaces; by rotational symmetry only the subspace dimension matters.
notes.extra: Geometry: Cochran's theorem is Pythagoras for Gaussians: split \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into orthogonal subspaces, and the squared lengths of the projections are independent \(\chi^2\) variables with degrees of freedom equal to the dimensions.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Give the geometric reading of the t-statistic and the F-statistic.
notes.back:
Both compare squared length per dimension in a "signal" subspace with squared length per dimension in the orthogonal "noise" (residual) subspace.
\(F = \dfrac{\|P_{\text{signal}}\,y\|^2/q}{\|P_{\text{resid}}\,y\|^2/(n-p)}\), and \(t^2 = F\) when \(q=1\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Under the null, y is pure isotropic noise and points in a random direction, so each dimension gets its fair share and \(F\approx 1\). A large F means y leans toward the signal subspace far more than a random direction would. t is essentially the cotangent of the angle between y and the noise subspace, scaled by \(\sqrt{n-p}\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Where does the probability mass of a standard Gaussian in \(d\) dimensions live when \(d\) is large?
notes.back: In a thin shell of radius \(\approx\sqrt{d}\) and thickness \(O(1)\). Almost no mass is near the mode at the origin, even though the density is highest there.
notes.extra: Geometry: Mass = density × volume. Density falls as \(e^{-r^2/2}\) but the volume of a shell grows as \(r^{d-1}\); their product peaks sharply at \(r=\sqrt{d-1}\). A high-dimensional Gaussian looks like a soap bubble, not a ball. This is the "typical set" and is why the mode is unrepresentative in Bayesian computation.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Name three geometric facts behind the "curse of dimensionality".
notes.back:
1. Volume concentrates near the surface: a fraction \(1-(1-\epsilon)^d \to 1\) of a ball lies in its outer \(\epsilon\)-shell.
2. Distances concentrate: nearest and farthest neighbour become nearly equidistant.
3. Random vectors are nearly orthogonal: \(\cos\theta \sim N(0, 1/d)\).
Consequence: local methods need \(n\) exponential in \(d\) to keep neighbourhoods local.
notes.extra: Geometry: To capture 10% of a unit hypercube's volume in 10 dimensions, a sub-cube needs side length \(0.1^{1/10}\approx 0.8\). "Local" neighbourhoods span 80% of every axis. The rescue is that real data lies near low-dimensional manifolds.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: State Jensen's inequality and its picture.
notes.back: For convex \(f\): \(f(E[X]) \le E[f(X)]\). Equality iff \(f\) is linear on the support of \(X\) (or \(X\) is constant).
notes.extra: Geometry: A chord of a convex function lies above the curve. \(E[f(X)]\) is a weighted average of points on the curve, so it sits on or above the curve evaluated at the average x. Underlies: KL divergence \(\ge 0\), the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), \(E[X^2]\ge E[X]^2\), and why the log of an average exceeds the average of logs.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Define the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. What does it measure and why is it not a distance?
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q) = E_p\!\left[\log\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right] \ge 0\).
It is the expected extra log-loss (extra code length) from using model \(q\) when the truth is \(p\). It is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality.
notes.extra: Geometry: Locally it behaves like a squared distance: \(\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+d\theta}) \approx \tfrac12\, d\theta^\top I(\theta)\, d\theta\) with \(I\) the Fisher information. So the Fisher information is the metric tensor of the curved "statistical manifold" and KL is its (asymmetric) squared-length surrogate.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Relate entropy, cross-entropy and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.
notes.back:
\(H(p,q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q)\), where \(H(p,q) = -E_p[\log q]\).
Since \(H(p)\) does not depend on the model, minimising cross-entropy = minimising KL = maximising likelihood.
notes.extra: Geometry: \(H(p)\) is the irreducible cost of the terrain; KL is the detour caused by a wrong map. Training can only shrink the detour.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: Which distributions are maximum-entropy under which constraints? (three classics)
notes.back:
Fixed support \([a,b]\) only: uniform.
Fixed mean on \([0,\infty)\): exponential.
Fixed mean and variance on \(\mathbb{R}\): Gaussian.
In general, constraining \(E[T(x)]\) yields the exponential family \(p(x)\propto \exp(\eta^\top T(x))\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Maximum entropy = the flattest, least committal distribution compatible with what you know. The Lagrange multipliers of the constraints become the natural parameters \(\eta\). This is why exponential families are the "default" models.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::01 Probability & Geometric Foundations
notes.front: State the delta method and its geometric content.
notes.back:
If \(\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta-\theta)\to N(0,\Sigma)\) and \(g\) is differentiable, then
\(\sqrt{n}\,(g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta)) \to N\!\left(0,\ \nabla g^\top \Sigma\, \nabla g\right)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: At scale \(1/\sqrt{n}\) the estimator's cloud is so small that \(g\) looks like its tangent plane. A linear map of a Gaussian is Gaussian, and the variance is scaled by the squared slope. Fails when the gradient is zero (then you need the second-order term and get a \(\chi^2\)-type limit).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Describe Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) as a geometric operation. What do the normal equations say?
notes.back: \(\hat y = X\hat\beta\) is the orthogonal projection of \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) onto the column space of \(X\). The normal equations \(X^\top(y - X\hat\beta)=0\) state that the residual is perpendicular to every column of \(X\). Solving gives \(\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The columns of X span a p-dimensional plane inside n-dimensional observation space. y floats above that plane; the fitted vector is its shadow under a light shining straight down. Minimising squared error = finding the closest point in the plane = dropping a perpendicular.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What is the hat matrix \(H\), and what are its three defining properties?
notes.back:
\(H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\), so \(\hat y = Hy\).
1. Symmetric: \(H^\top=H\) (orthogonal, not oblique, projection).
2. Idempotent: \(H^2=H\) (projecting twice changes nothing).
3. \(\mathrm{tr}(H)=\mathrm{rank}(X)=p\) (dimension of the subspace).
\(I-H\) projects onto the residual space of dimension \(n-p\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Eigenvalues of a projection are only 1 (directions inside the plane, kept) and 0 (directions perpendicular, killed). The trace counts the ones: model degrees of freedom.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What is \(R^2\) geometrically?
notes.back:
\(R^2 = \cos^2\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the centered response \(y-\bar y\mathbf 1\) and the centered fitted vector \(\hat y - \bar y\mathbf 1\).
Equivalently \(R^2 = \|\hat y-\bar y\|^2/\|y-\bar y\|^2\) from the right triangle total = explained + residual.
notes.extra: Geometry: Adding any column to X can only enlarge the subspace, so the projection can only get closer to y: \(R^2\) never decreases, even for pure-noise predictors. A random extra direction captures on average \(1/(n-1)\) of the remaining squared length, which is what adjusted \(R^2\) corrects for.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Regression has two dual pictures. What are the "row picture" and the "column picture"?
notes.back:
Row picture (scatterplot): \(n\) points in \(\mathbb{R}^{p+1}\); fit a hyperplane minimising vertical distances.
Column picture: \(p\) predictor vectors and one response vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\); project \(y\) onto their span.
notes.extra: Geometry: The row picture is good for intuition about outliers, leverage and nonlinearity. The column picture is where inference lives: orthogonality, degrees of freedom, collinearity, and F-tests are all statements about subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: State the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (FWL) theorem. What does it say about the meaning of a multiple-regression coefficient?
notes.back:
The coefficient on \(x_j\) in a multiple regression equals the coefficient from regressing (residual of \(y\) on the other predictors) on (residual of \(x_j\) on the other predictors).
So \(\hat\beta_j\) uses only the part of \(x_j\) that is orthogonal to all other predictors.
notes.extra: Geometry: "Controlling for Z" literally means projecting Z out of both x and y, then doing simple regression in the leftover space. If \(x_j\) is almost inside the span of the others, the leftover sliver is tiny and the estimate is noisy.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What is multicollinearity geometrically, and what is the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)?
notes.back:
Predictor columns are nearly linearly dependent (nearly parallel). The projection \(\hat y\) is still stable, but its coordinates \(\hat\beta\) in that skewed basis are not.
\(\mathrm{VIF}_j = \dfrac{1}{1-R_j^2}\), where \(R_j^2\) is from regressing \(x_j\) on the other predictors; \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)\) is multiplied by it.
notes.extra: Geometry: Locating a point using two nearly parallel rulers: a tiny wobble of the point produces huge, offsetting changes in both readings. Predictions stay fine; individual coefficients become meaningless. By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell view, \(1-R_j^2\) is the squared sine of the angle between \(x_j\) and the span of the rest.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: State the Gauss-Markov theorem and its assumptions.
notes.back: If \(y=X\beta+\varepsilon\) with \(E[\varepsilon]=0\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 I\) (uncorrelated, homoskedastic; normality not needed), then Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE): minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators.
notes.extra: Geometry: Every linear unbiased estimator is a projection onto col(X), possibly an oblique one. With spherical noise, the perpendicular projection is the one that lets through the least noise; any slanted projection drags in extra noise from the residual space. Note the class is narrow: biased estimators (ridge) can beat OLS in mean squared error.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Give \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)\) for Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and interpret the shape of the confidence region.
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta) = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\).
The confidence ellipsoid for \(\beta\) is the inverse of the data cloud's shape: long where the predictors have little spread, short where they have much spread.
notes.extra: Geometry: A plank resting on widely spaced supports is stable; on supports bunched together it wobbles. Spread in X pins the hyperplane down in that direction. Collinear predictors give a data cloud that is thin in one direction, hence a confidence ellipsoid that is long in that direction (typically along \(\beta_1+\beta_2=\) const: the sum is known, the split is not).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Under what model is Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE)? What changes with other noise models?
notes.back:
With \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2I)\) the negative log-likelihood is \(\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y-X\beta\|^2 + \text{const}\), so MLE = OLS.
Laplace noise gives least absolute deviations (median regression); Student-t noise gives robust regression that downweights outliers.
notes.extra: Geometry: The loss function is the negative log of the noise density. Squared loss means you believe in thin Gaussian tails, so an outlier 10 standard deviations away is "impossible" and the fit contorts itself to explain it.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: State the omitted variable bias formula.
notes.back:
True model \(y = x\beta + z\gamma + \varepsilon\); regressing on \(x\) alone gives
\(E[\hat\beta_{\text{short}}] = \beta + \gamma\,\delta\), where \(\delta\) is the coefficient from regressing \(z\) on \(x\).
Bias needs both: \(z\) affects \(y\) (\(\gamma\ne 0\)) and \(z\) correlates with \(x\) (\(\delta\ne 0\)).
notes.extra: Geometry: If z is left out, its effect does not vanish: the part of z that is parallel to x gets projected onto x and credited to it. Only when z is perpendicular to x does its contribution fall harmlessly into the residual.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Give the ridge regression estimator and describe what it does in the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) basis of \(X\).
notes.back:
\(\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\).
With \(X=UDV^\top\): each component of the fit along \(u_j\) is multiplied by the shrinkage factor \(\dfrac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\lambda}\).
High-variance directions (\(d_j^2\gg\lambda\)) are barely touched; low-variance directions are shrunk toward zero.
notes.extra: Geometry: Ridge distrusts exactly the directions where the data is thin and the OLS coefficient is therefore noisy. It is a "soft" version of principal component regression, which uses a hard 0/1 cutoff instead of a smooth factor.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Why does the lasso (L1 penalty) produce exactly-zero coefficients while ridge (L2 penalty) does not?
notes.back:
Penalised form is equivalent to minimising the residual sum of squares subject to \(\|\beta\|_1\le t\) (lasso) or \(\|\beta\|_2\le t\) (ridge). The solution is where the elliptical loss contours first touch the constraint region.
The L1 ball is a diamond with corners on the axes; contours generically hit a corner or edge, where some coordinates are exactly 0. The L2 ball is smooth, so the touching point is generic (no zeros).
notes.extra: Geometry: In d dimensions the L1 ball is a cross-polytope whose corners, edges and low-dimensional faces all lie in coordinate subspaces, and they "stick out" so they are hit first. Analytically: the L1 subgradient at 0 is the whole interval [-λ, λ], so a coefficient stays at 0 until its correlation with the residual exceeds λ.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What Bayesian priors correspond to ridge and lasso, and what is \(\lambda\) in those terms?
notes.back:
Both are Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimates under Gaussian noise:
Ridge: Gaussian prior \(\beta_j\sim N(0,\tau^2)\), with \(\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2\).
Lasso: Laplace (double-exponential) prior, \(\lambda \propto \sigma^2/b\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Penalty = negative log prior. λ is a noise-to-signal ratio: noisy data or a tight prior means more shrinkage. Caveat: the lasso's sparsity is a property of the MAP point only; the full Laplace posterior puts zero mass on exact zeros. Truly sparse Bayesian answers need spike-and-slab or horseshoe priors.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Define effective degrees of freedom for a linear smoother \(\hat y = S y\), and give its value for ridge regression.
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{df} = \mathrm{tr}(S) = \sum_i \partial\hat y_i/\partial y_i\) (how much the fit chases each observation).
Ridge: \(\mathrm{df}(\lambda) = \sum_j \dfrac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\lambda}\), falling from \(p\) at \(\lambda=0\) to \(0\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
notes.extra: Geometry: For a true projection the trace counts dimensions (eigenvalues 1). A smoother has eigenvalues between 0 and 1: it uses each direction only fractionally, so the "dimension" of the model becomes a continuous dial.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: State the bias-variance decomposition of expected squared prediction error at a point \(x\).
notes.back:
\(E[(y-\hat f(x))^2] = \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}} + \underbrace{(E\hat f(x)-f(x))^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\hat f(x))}_{\text{variance}}\)
The expectation is over training sets and noise.
notes.extra: Geometry: Picture the model class as a surface in function space. Bias = distance from the truth to the nearest point on the surface. Variance = how much your estimate scatters around on the surface as the training sample changes. A bigger surface gets closer to the truth but gives the estimate more room to wander.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What is leverage \(h_{ii}\) and how does it combine with the residual to give influence (Cook's distance)?
notes.back:
\(h_{ii}\) is the i-th diagonal of the hat matrix: \(\partial\hat y_i/\partial y_i\), between 0 and 1, averaging \(p/n\). It depends only on X: how far \(x_i\) is from the centre of the predictor cloud (a Mahalanobis distance).
Cook's distance \(D_i \propto r_i^2\,\dfrac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}}\): influence = large residual × high leverage.
notes.extra: Geometry: A seesaw. A point far out on the plank (high leverage) can tilt the line massively, and because it pulls the line toward itself it may show a small residual. An outlier near the fulcrum barely tilts anything.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What breaks under heteroskedasticity, and what are the two standard fixes?
notes.back:
Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) stays unbiased and consistent but is no longer efficient, and the usual standard errors are wrong.
Fix 1: keep OLS, use heteroskedasticity-robust "sandwich" standard errors \((X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\hat\Omega X(X^\top X)^{-1}\).
Fix 2: Generalized Least Squares (GLS), \(\hat\beta=(X^\top\Omega^{-1}X)^{-1}X^\top\Omega^{-1}y\).
notes.extra: Geometry: GLS is OLS after whitening the noise: a perpendicular projection in the metric defined by \(\Omega^{-1}\). When noise is an ellipsoid rather than a sphere, "perpendicular" must be measured with the Mahalanobis ruler; precise observations get more say.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: Why does regression to the mean occur, and where is the regression line relative to the data ellipse?
notes.back:
In standardised units the regression slope is \(r\), with \(|r|<1\): a predictor value \(z\) standard deviations from the mean predicts a response only \(r z\) standard deviations from its mean. It is a property of imperfect correlation, not a causal force.
The regression line of y on x passes through the points where the ellipse has vertical tangents; it is flatter than the ellipse's major axis.
notes.extra: Geometry: Slice the ellipse vertically at a given x; the conditional mean is the midpoint of that slice. Those midpoints trace a line that is shallower than the major axis. Regressing x on y instead gives a different line (through the horizontal tangents), steeper than the major axis.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: How does the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) line differ from the first principal component of the same 2-D data?
notes.back:
OLS minimises vertical squared distances (error only in y; asymmetric in x and y).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) minimises perpendicular squared distances (total least squares; symmetric) and gives the major axis of the data ellipse.
The OLS line is always flatter (attenuated toward zero slope) than the PCA axis.
notes.extra: Geometry: If x is itself measured with error, OLS suffers "attenuation bias": the slope shrinks by the reliability ratio \(\sigma_x^2/(\sigma_x^2+\sigma_{\text{error}}^2)\). Noise in x stretches the cloud horizontally, flattening the vertical-slice midpoints.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What does the F-test for nested linear models measure geometrically?
notes.back:
Small model space \(V_0\subset V_1\) big model space. Decompose \(y\) into three orthogonal pieces: projection on \(V_0\), projection on \(V_1\ominus V_0\) (dimension \(q\)), and residual (dimension \(n-p\)).
\(F = \dfrac{\|P_{V_1\ominus V_0}\,y\|^2/q}{\|(I-P_{V_1})\,y\|^2/(n-p)}\)
notes.extra: Geometry: Does y lean into the extra q dimensions more than isotropic noise would by chance? Under the null each dimension receives about \(\sigma^2\) of squared length, so the ratio hovers around 1.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: When \(p>n\), which solution does the pseudoinverse (and gradient descent from zero) pick among the infinitely many interpolating solutions?
notes.back: The minimum L2-norm interpolator \(\hat\beta = X^{+}y = X^\top(XX^\top)^{-1}y\). It lies in the row space of \(X\), which is also where gradient descent started at 0 stays forever, since every gradient \(X^\top(\cdot)\) lies in the row space.
notes.extra: Geometry: The interpolating solutions form an affine subspace (a flat sheet not through the origin). The minimum-norm one is the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to that sheet. This is "ridgeless" regression, the \(\lambda\to0^+\) limit of ridge, and the basic mechanism of implicit regularisation.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::02 Linear Regression
notes.front: What problem do Instrumental Variables (IV) solve, and what is Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) geometrically?
notes.back:
When a regressor \(x\) is correlated with the error (confounding, reverse causation, measurement error), Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) is inconsistent. An instrument \(z\) must be (1) relevant: correlated with \(x\); (2) excluded/exogenous: affects \(y\) only through \(x\).
2SLS: project \(x\) onto the span of \(z\), then regress \(y\) on that projection: \(\hat\beta=(X^\top P_Z X)^{-1}X^\top P_Z y\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Split x into a clean part (lying in the instrument's direction, orthogonal to the error) and a contaminated part. IV keeps only the clean sliver. If the instrument is weak the sliver is tiny, and the estimate is noisy and biased toward OLS.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Show that Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) is a Kullback-Leibler (KL) projection.
notes.back:
\(\frac1n\sum_i\log p_\theta(x_i) \to E_{p^*}[\log p_\theta] = -H(p^*) - \mathrm{KL}(p^*\,\|\,p_\theta)\).
So maximising likelihood = minimising \(\mathrm{KL}(\hat p_{\text{data}}\,\|\,p_\theta)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The model family is a curved surface (manifold) inside the space of all distributions. The empirical distribution is a point off that surface. MLE finds the closest point on the surface, with KL as the notion of "closest". If the truth is not on the surface (misspecification), MLE converges to the KL-nearest point rather than to nonsense.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Define the score function. What are its mean and variance at the true parameter?
notes.back:
\(s(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \log p(x\mid\theta)\).
\(E_\theta[s(\theta)] = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}_\theta[s(\theta)] = I(\theta)\), the Fisher information.
notes.extra: Geometry: The score is the slope of the log-likelihood hill. At the true parameter, individual observations push up- and downhill with equal expected force, so the pushes cancel on average. The size of those pushes (their variance) tells you how loudly the data speaks about θ.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Give the two equivalent definitions of Fisher information and its geometric meaning.
notes.back:
\(I(\theta) = E\!\left[s\,s^\top\right] = -E\!\left[\nabla^2_\theta \log p(x\mid\theta)\right]\)
(variance of the score = expected curvature of the log-likelihood). Information from independent observations adds: \(I_n = nI_1\).
notes.extra: Geometry: A sharply peaked log-likelihood (high curvature) pins the parameter down; a flat ridge does not. Fisher information is also the Riemannian metric on the model manifold: it converts parameter steps into "how distinguishable are the two distributions".

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: State the Cramér-Rao lower bound.
notes.back:
For any unbiased estimator \(\hat\theta\): \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta) \succeq I_n(\theta)^{-1}\) (scalar case: \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge 1/(nI_1(\theta))\)).
The Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) attains it asymptotically.
notes.extra: Geometry: Variance bound = inverse curvature. It is Cauchy-Schwarz in the Hilbert space of random variables: an unbiased estimator must have covariance exactly 1 with the score, and for fixed inner product the norm is minimised by being parallel to the score.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: State the asymptotic distribution of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) and the core idea of the proof.
notes.back:
\(\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta-\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} N\!\left(0,\ I(\theta_0)^{-1}\right)\) under regularity conditions.
Proof idea: Taylor-expand the score around \(\theta_0\): \(0 = s_n(\hat\theta)\approx s_n(\theta_0) - nI\,(\hat\theta-\theta_0)\). The score is a sum (Central Limit Theorem), the Hessian is an average (Law of Large Numbers).
notes.extra: Geometry: With lots of data, the log-likelihood near its peak becomes an exact downward paraboloid whose curvature is \(nI\). A paraboloid log-density is a Gaussian. The noisy score shifts the paraboloid's peak sideways by (noise)/(curvature).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Name the three classical likelihood-based tests and what each measures on the log-likelihood curve.
notes.back:
Testing \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\):
Wald: horizontal distance \(\hat\theta-\theta_0\), scaled by curvature at \(\hat\theta\).
Likelihood Ratio (LR): vertical drop \(2[\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta_0)]\).
Score (Lagrange multiplier): slope at \(\theta_0\), scaled by curvature at \(\theta_0\).
All three are asymptotically \(\chi^2\) and equivalent.
notes.extra: Geometry: On an exact parabola, horizontal distance, vertical drop and slope carry identical information, so the tests agree. They diverge in finite samples precisely to the extent the log-likelihood is not quadratic. Wald is not invariant to reparameterisation; LR is. Score needs only the null model to be fitted.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: State Wilks' theorem.
notes.back:
For nested regular models, under \(H_0\): \(2\left[\ell(\hat\theta_{\text{full}}) - \ell(\hat\theta_{\text{null}})\right] \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_q\), with \(q\) the number of constrained parameters.
Fails when the null is on the boundary of the parameter space (e.g. variance component = 0, mixture weight = 0) or parameters are unidentified under the null.
notes.extra: Geometry: Near the peak the log-likelihood is a paraboloid; the drop from the unconstrained peak to the constrained peak is the squared length (in Fisher metric) of a Gaussian vector's component in the q forbidden directions: a \(\chi^2_q\). Generalises the linear-model F-test.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: What exactly is a p-value, and name three things it is not.
notes.back:
\(p = P(\text{test statistic at least this extreme}\mid H_0)\). It is computed assuming the null, and under the null it is uniformly distributed on [0,1].
It is not: (1) \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\); (2) the probability the result is due to chance; (3) a measure of effect size or importance.
notes.extra: Geometry: It is a tail area under the null's sampling distribution. Converting to \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\) requires a prior and the alternative's likelihood: \(p=0.05\) often corresponds to a posterior null probability of 20-50% for plausible priors.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Distinguish a 95% confidence interval from a 95% credible interval.
notes.back:
Confidence interval: a random interval produced by a procedure that covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. The probability statement is about the procedure.
Credible interval: a fixed interval containing 95% of the posterior mass of the (random) parameter given this dataset and prior.
notes.extra: Geometry: They coincide numerically for location problems with flat priors and asymptotically (Bernstein-von Mises), which is why the misreading usually goes unpunished. They diverge with strong priors, small samples, boundaries, or optional stopping.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Define a sufficient statistic and state the Fisher-Neyman factorisation criterion.
notes.back:
\(T(x)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the distribution of \(x\) given \(T(x)\) does not depend on \(\theta\).
Criterion: \(p(x\mid\theta) = g(T(x),\theta)\,h(x)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The level sets of T partition sample space into contours. Which contour you land on carries all the information about θ; where you are within the contour is pure noise. Lossless data compression for inference. Fixed-dimension sufficient statistics for all n exist essentially only in exponential families (Pitman-Koopman-Darmois).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Write the exponential family form and state what the derivatives of the log-partition function give.
notes.back:
\(p(x\mid\eta) = h(x)\exp\!\left(\eta^\top T(x) - A(\eta)\right)\).
\(\nabla A(\eta) = E[T(x)]\), \(\nabla^2 A(\eta) = \mathrm{Cov}[T(x)] = I(\eta)\).
So \(A\) is convex, the log-likelihood is concave in \(\eta\), and the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) is moment matching: \(E_{\hat\eta}[T] = \frac1n\sum T(x_i)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Two coordinate systems on the same manifold: natural parameters η and mean parameters μ = ∇A(η), linked by a Legendre transform (convex duality). The manifold is "flat" in each. This dual flatness is the core of information geometry.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: What is the bootstrap principle? When does it fail?
notes.back:
Plug-in principle: approximate the unknown distribution \(F\) by the empirical \(\hat F\), and approximate "sampling from \(F\)" by resampling with replacement from the data. The variability of \(\hat\theta^*\) around \(\hat\theta\) mimics the variability of \(\hat\theta\) around \(\theta\).
Fails for: extremes (max/min), parameters on a boundary, heavy tails with infinite variance, dependent data unless blocks are resampled.
notes.extra: Geometry: Analogy of worlds: real world (population → sample) is to bootstrap world (sample → resample). We cannot rerun the first arrow, so we rerun the second, which we fully control, and transfer the error distribution back.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Contrast Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) control with False Discovery Rate (FDR) control.
notes.back:
FWER = P(at least one false rejection). Bonferroni: test each at \(\alpha/m\). Strict; power collapses as \(m\) grows.
FDR = E[false rejections / total rejections]. Benjamini-Hochberg: sort p-values, reject all up to the largest \(k\) with \(p_{(k)}\le \frac{k}{m}\alpha\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Plot sorted p-values against rank. Null p-values are uniform, so they hug the diagonal of slope 1/m. Benjamini-Hochberg draws a line of slope α/m from the origin and rejects everything before the last point below the line: the early p-values that dip too far under the uniform diagonal to be nulls.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: State the Neyman-Pearson lemma.
notes.back: For testing simple \(H_0: p_0\) vs simple \(H_1: p_1\), the most powerful test at level \(\alpha\) rejects when the likelihood ratio \(\Lambda(x)=p_1(x)/p_0(x)\) exceeds a threshold \(k\) chosen to give size \(\alpha\).
notes.extra: Geometry: You have a budget of α of null probability to spend on a rejection region. Spend it where you get the most alternative probability per unit of null probability: "best bang for the buck" is points ranked by \(p_1/p_0\). A fractional knapsack problem.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: What determines statistical power, and how does sample size enter?
notes.back:
Power = P(reject \(H_0\mid H_1\) true). It increases with effect size \(\delta\), sample size \(n\), and level \(\alpha\); it decreases with noise \(\sigma\).
For a z-test: power \(\approx \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma} - z_{1-\alpha}\right)\). Required \(n \propto \sigma^2/\delta^2\): halving the detectable effect costs 4× the data.
notes.extra: Geometry: Two bell curves (sampling distributions of the estimate under null and alternative) with centres δ apart and widths \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\). More data does not move them; it makes them thinner until they stop overlapping.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: What does the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) converge to under model misspecification, and what is its asymptotic covariance?
notes.back:
To the pseudo-true parameter \(\theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{true}}\,\|\,p_\theta)\).
Covariance is the sandwich \(A^{-1}BA^{-1}/n\), with \(A = -E[\nabla^2\log p_\theta]\) (curvature) and \(B = E[s\,s^\top]\) (score variance).
When the model is correct, \(A=B=I(\theta)\) and the sandwich collapses to \(I^{-1}/n\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The information equality (curvature = score variance) is a signature of a correct model. When it fails, curvature alone misjudges the uncertainty; you must measure the actual spread of the score pushes (the "meat") and convert via the curvature (the "bread").

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: What is the James-Stein phenomenon, and what is its geometric explanation?
notes.back: For \(x\sim N(\theta, I_d)\) with \(d\ge3\), the estimator \(\hat\theta_{JS} = \left(1-\dfrac{d-2}{\|x\|^2}\right)x\) has strictly lower total mean squared error than the Maximum Likelihood Estimator \(x\), for every \(\theta\). Shrinking unrelated means toward a common point helps.
notes.extra: Geometry: \(E\|x\|^2 = \|\theta\|^2 + d\). The noise is almost surely nearly orthogonal to θ in high dimensions, so the observed vector is the hypotenuse of a right triangle: systematically too long. Shrinking it corrects the length. This is the root of ridge, hierarchical models and empirical Bayes.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Explain the Expectation-Maximisation (EM) algorithm via a lower bound.
notes.back:
For any distribution \(q(z)\) over latent variables:
\(\log p(x\mid\theta) = \underbrace{E_q\!\left[\log\tfrac{p(x,z\mid\theta)}{q(z)}\right]}_{\text{lower bound } \mathcal{L}(q,\theta)} + \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x,\theta)\right)\)
E-step: set \(q = p(z\mid x,\theta_{\text{old}})\) so the bound touches the log-likelihood.
M-step: maximise \(\mathcal L\) over \(\theta\). The likelihood never decreases.
notes.extra: Geometry: Coordinate ascent on \(\mathcal L(q,\theta)\). Picture a hard-to-climb curve; at the current point fit a smooth surrogate that lies under it and touches it, jump to the surrogate's top, repeat (minorise-maximise). Variational inference is the same picture with q restricted to a tractable family so the bound never quite touches.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: Contrast the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{AIC} = -2\ell + 2k\): estimates expected out-of-sample Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence; targets prediction; asymptotically equivalent to leave-one-out cross-validation; tends to overfit slightly.
\(\mathrm{BIC} = -2\ell + k\log n\): Laplace approximation to \(-2\log\) marginal likelihood; targets identifying the true model; consistent if the truth is among the candidates.
notes.extra: Geometry: The "+2k" is an optimism correction: each fitted parameter lets the in-sample likelihood climb by about 1 unit (half a \(\chi^2_1\)) by fitting noise, and out of sample you lose the same again. BIC's log n grows because the Occam penalty of a prior volume collapsing to a posterior volume scales as \(n^{-k/2}\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::03 Likelihood & Frequentist Inference
notes.front: What is the leave-one-out cross-validation shortcut for linear smoothers?
notes.back:
For \(\hat y = Sy\) (Ordinary Least Squares, ridge, splines, kernel ridge): the leave-one-out residual is
\(e_{(i)} = \dfrac{y_i - \hat y_i}{1 - S_{ii}}\).
So leave-one-out error needs one fit, not \(n\). Generalised Cross-Validation (GCV) replaces \(S_{ii}\) by the average \(\mathrm{tr}(S)/n\).
notes.extra: Geometry: \(S_{ii}\) is the self-influence (leverage) of point i: the fraction of its own fitted value that it supplies. Removing the point inflates its residual by exactly the factor that undoes this self-help. High-leverage points flatter themselves most.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What are the three components of a Generalized Linear Model (GLM)?
notes.back:
1. Random component: \(y\) from an exponential-family distribution (Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, Gamma).
2. Linear predictor: \(\eta = X\beta\).
3. Link function: \(g(\mu)=\eta\), where \(\mu=E[y\mid x]\).
The model is linear on the link scale, not on the scale of the data.
notes.extra: Geometry: Linear regression lets a flat plane live in data space. A GLM keeps the flat plane but puts it in a warped coordinate system (log-odds, log-rate) chosen so that the plane can never predict an impossible mean (a probability of 1.3, a negative count).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What is special about the canonical link in a Generalized Linear Model (GLM)? Give the score equations.
notes.back:
The canonical link sets the natural parameter equal to the linear predictor (\(\theta=\eta\)): logit for Bernoulli, log for Poisson, identity for Gaussian.
Then the score equations are \(X^\top(y-\hat\mu)=0\), the log-likelihood is concave, and \(X^\top y\) is sufficient.
notes.extra: Geometry: Same orthogonality condition as Ordinary Least Squares: the residual is perpendicular to every predictor column. The only difference is that \(\hat\mu\) lives on a curved surface \(\{g^{-1}(X\beta)\}\) rather than a flat subspace, so the "projection" must be found iteratively.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: In logistic regression, what is the geometry of the decision boundary and of the coefficient vector?
notes.back:
\(\log\dfrac{p}{1-p} = w^\top x + b\). The boundary \(p=0.5\) is the hyperplane \(w^\top x+b=0\).
\(w\) is the normal vector to that hyperplane; \(\|w\|\) sets how fast the probability changes as you move away from it. \(e^{w_j}\) is the odds ratio per unit of \(x_j\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The probability surface is a sigmoid ramp extruded along the hyperplane. The signed distance to the boundary is \((w^\top x+b)/\|w\|\); multiply by \(\|w\|\) to get log-odds. Large \(\|w\|\): a cliff. Small \(\|w\|\): a gentle slope.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What happens to the logistic regression Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) under perfect separation, and why?
notes.back:
It does not exist: \(\|\hat w\|\to\infty\). If a hyperplane separates the classes, scaling \(w\) up always increases the likelihood, pushing all fitted probabilities toward 0 or 1. Symptoms: huge coefficients, huge standard errors, convergence warnings.
Fixes: L2/L1 penalty, Firth's bias-reduced likelihood, weakly informative priors.
notes.extra: Geometry: The direction of w converges (interestingly, to the maximum-margin separator when trained by gradient descent) while its length diverges: the sigmoid ramp steepens into a step function.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: How is a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) fitted? Describe Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS).
notes.back:
IRLS is Newton-Raphson / Fisher scoring on the log-likelihood. Each step solves a weighted least squares problem
\(\beta^{\text{new}} = (X^\top WX)^{-1}X^\top Wz\)
with working response \(z = \eta + (y-\mu)\,g'(\mu)\) and weights \(W = 1/(V(\mu)\,g'(\mu)^2)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Approximate the curved mean surface by its tangent plane at the current fit, project onto that plane (with a metric that weights observations by their local precision), move, re-linearise. A sequence of ordinary projections that converges to the curved one.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What is deviance in a Generalized Linear Model (GLM)?
notes.back:
\(D = 2\left[\ell(\text{saturated model}) - \ell(\text{fitted model})\right]\).
For Gaussian errors it equals the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)/\(\sigma^2\). Differences in deviance between nested models are likelihood-ratio statistics, asymptotically \(\chi^2\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Deviance is twice the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the data (saturated fit) to the model fit: the GLM's replacement for squared Euclidean distance. For Gaussians, KL between two means is squared distance, which is why RSS is a special case.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What is overdispersion in count models and how do you handle it?
notes.back:
Poisson forces \(\mathrm{Var}(y)=\mu\). Real counts usually have \(\mathrm{Var}(y)>\mu\) (unobserved heterogeneity, clustering). Coefficients remain roughly fine but standard errors are too small.
Fixes: quasi-Poisson (estimate a dispersion factor \(\phi\)), Negative Binomial (\(\mathrm{Var}=\mu+\mu^2/k\)), observation-level random effects.
Diagnostic: residual deviance / degrees of freedom \(\gg 1\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The Negative Binomial is a Poisson whose rate is itself Gamma-distributed: a mixture. Mixing always adds variance (law of total variance: variance of the conditional mean is piled on top).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What is partial pooling in a hierarchical (mixed-effects) model? Give the shrinkage formula for a group mean.
notes.back:
Group effects are modelled as draws from a common distribution, \(\alpha_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)\). The estimate for group \(j\) is a precision-weighted compromise:
\(\hat\alpha_j = \lambda_j\,\bar y_j + (1-\lambda_j)\,\hat\mu,\qquad \lambda_j = \dfrac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j}\).
Small or noisy groups are shrunk strongly toward the grand mean.
notes.extra: Geometry: Between "no pooling" (each group alone: high variance) and "complete pooling" (one mean for all: high bias) lies a continuum; the data choose the position through \(\tau^2\). Each estimate slides along the segment from its own mean toward the grand mean. It is James-Stein with the shrinkage amount learned.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: How do smoothing splines / Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) fit nonlinear functions while remaining "linear models"?
notes.back:
Expand each predictor in a basis \(f(x)=\sum_k\beta_k b_k(x)\) (B-splines), then penalise roughness:
minimise \(\|y-B\beta\|^2 + \lambda\int f''(x)^2dx = \|y-B\beta\|^2+\lambda\,\beta^\top\Omega\beta\).
This is generalised ridge regression; \(\lambda\) chosen by cross-validation or Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML).
notes.extra: Geometry: Still a projection-like linear smoother \(\hat y = S_\lambda y\) in a richer column space. The penalty leaves the straight-line component untouched (zero curvature) and shrinks wigglier basis directions progressively harder: a low-pass filter.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: In kernel / local regression, what role does the bandwidth \(h\) play?
notes.back:
The estimate at \(x_0\) is a locally weighted average (Nadaraya-Watson) or local linear fit with weights \(K((x_i-x_0)/h)\).
Small \(h\): low bias, high variance (wiggly). Large \(h\): high bias, low variance (flat).
Optimal \(h\propto n^{-1/5}\) in 1-D, giving error rate \(n^{-4/5}\); in \(d\) dimensions the rate degrades to \(n^{-4/(4+d)}\).
notes.extra: Geometry: A sliding window. Bias comes from curvature of the truth inside the window; variance from how few points the window contains. The d-dimensional rate is the curse of dimensionality stated as a theorem.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: In survival analysis, define the hazard function and explain how the Cox model handles censoring without specifying a baseline.
notes.back:
Hazard \(h(t) = \lim_{dt\to0} P(t\le T<t+dt\mid T\ge t)/dt\), the instantaneous failure rate among survivors.
Cox: \(h(t\mid x) = h_0(t)\exp(x^\top\beta)\). The partial likelihood multiplies, over event times, \(\dfrac{\exp(x_i^\top\beta)}{\sum_{j\in\text{risk set}}\exp(x_j^\top\beta)}\); \(h_0\) cancels. Censored subjects contribute to risk sets until they drop out.
notes.extra: Geometry: At each event time, ask: "of everyone still at risk, how surprising is it that this person failed?" That is a softmax over the risk set. Only the ordering of events matters, not the clock times.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What loss does quantile regression minimise, and why does it yield a quantile?
notes.back:
The pinball (check) loss \(\rho_\tau(u) = u\,(\tau - \mathbb 1[u<0])\): under-predictions cost \(\tau\) per unit, over-predictions cost \(1-\tau\).
At the minimum the subgradients balance: a fraction \(\tau\) of the mass lies below the prediction. \(\tau=0.5\) gives the median (absolute loss).
notes.extra: Geometry: A tilted V. Squared loss balances like a centre of mass (mean); absolute loss balances by head-count (median); tilting the V moves the head-count balance point to any quantile.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: Explain Simpson's paradox geometrically.
notes.back:
A trend that holds within every subgroup reverses when groups are pooled, because group membership is associated with both \(x\) and \(y\).
Pooled slope = a weighted mix of the within-group slopes and the between-group slope (the slope through the group centroids), and the two can have opposite signs.
notes.extra: Geometry: Several small clouds each tilting upward, but arranged in a staircase going downward. The pooled fit follows the staircase. Which slope is "right" is a causal question (is the group variable a confounder or a mediator/collider?), not a statistical one.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: For causal adjustment, how do you treat a confounder, a mediator and a collider?
notes.back:
Confounder (\(X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y\)): adjust for it; it opens a spurious back-door path.
Mediator (\(X\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y\)): do not adjust if you want the total effect.
Collider (\(X\rightarrow C\leftarrow Y\)): do not adjust; conditioning on it (or selecting on it) creates a spurious association.
notes.extra: Geometry: Collider bias as slicing: talent and looks are independent in the population (a round cloud). Condition on "became an actor" = talent + looks above a threshold: you keep only the upper-right corner beyond a diagonal line, and inside that slice the two are negatively correlated.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: State the potential-outcomes definition of the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) and why randomisation identifies it.
notes.back:
Each unit has \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\); only one is observed. \(\mathrm{ATE}=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]\).
Naive difference = ATE + selection bias: \(E[Y(0)\mid T=1]-E[Y(0)\mid T=0]\).
Randomisation makes \(T\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\), so selection bias is zero. Observational studies need conditional ignorability \(T\perp Y(t)\mid X\) plus overlap \(0<P(T=1\mid X)<1\).
notes.extra: Geometry: A missing-data problem: half of every row of the potential-outcomes table is blank. Randomisation guarantees the blanks are missing completely at random.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::04 GLMs, Hierarchical & Causal
notes.front: What is a propensity score and why is it enough to adjust for it alone?
notes.back:
\(e(x)=P(T=1\mid X=x)\). Rosenbaum-Rubin: if treatment is ignorable given \(X\), it is ignorable given the scalar \(e(X)\); \(e(X)\) is a balancing score (\(X\perp T\mid e(X)\)).
Used for matching, stratification, or Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW): weight treated by \(1/e\), controls by \(1/(1-e)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Collapses a high-dimensional covariate space to one axis along which treatment assignment varies. Within a slice of constant propensity, treatment is as good as a coin flip. Weights explode when e is near 0 or 1: those are regions with no overlap, where the data cannot speak.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: State Bayes' theorem for parameters and describe the update geometrically.
notes.back:
\(p(\theta\mid x) = \dfrac{p(x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(x)} \propto \text{likelihood}\times\text{prior}\).
In log space: log-posterior = log-likelihood + log-prior + const.
notes.extra: Geometry: Pointwise multiplication of two surfaces over parameter space, then renormalising. The posterior is high only where both are high. For Gaussians, adding two downward parabolas gives a parabola whose curvature is the sum: precisions add, and the peak lands between the two peaks, nearer the sharper one.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is a conjugate prior? Work the Beta-Binomial case.
notes.back:
A prior family that is closed under the likelihood's update, so the posterior has the same form.
Prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\), data \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials, posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,\ b+n-k)\).
Posterior mean \(\dfrac{a+k}{a+b+n}\): a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample proportion.
notes.extra: Geometry: The hyperparameters are pseudo-counts: the prior behaves like a+b imaginary earlier trials. Conjugacy exists exactly for exponential families: the prior is shaped like a likelihood from fictitious data, so updating just adds sufficient statistics.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: Normal likelihood with known variance and Normal prior: give the posterior mean and precision.
notes.back:
Prior \(N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)\), data mean \(\bar x\) from \(n\) observations with variance \(\sigma^2\).
Posterior precision: \(\dfrac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \dfrac{1}{\tau_0^2}+\dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}\).
Posterior mean: \(\mu_n = \dfrac{\mu_0/\tau_0^2 + n\bar x/\sigma^2}{1/\tau_0^2+n/\sigma^2}\), a precision-weighted average.
notes.extra: Geometry: The posterior mean is the centre of mass of two weights placed at the prior mean and at the data mean, with masses equal to their precisions. As n grows the data's mass dominates and the prior is forgotten.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is the posterior predictive distribution and how does it differ from a plug-in prediction?
notes.back:
\(p(\tilde x\mid x) = \int p(\tilde x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta\).
It averages predictions over parameter uncertainty, so it is wider than \(p(\tilde x\mid\hat\theta)\). Normal example: predictive variance \(=\sigma^2+\tau_n^2\) (noise + parameter uncertainty).
notes.extra: Geometry: A plug-in forecast is one curve; the posterior predictive is a blurred bundle of curves. Law of total variance: aleatoric (within-model noise) plus epistemic (which model). Only the second shrinks with data.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is the marginal likelihood (evidence) and how does it implement an automatic Occam's razor?
notes.back:
\(p(x\mid M)=\int p(x\mid\theta,M)\,p(\theta\mid M)\,d\theta\): the prior-weighted average fit, i.e. the probability the model assigned to the observed data before seeing it.
A flexible model must spread its unit of probability mass over many possible datasets, so it assigns less to any particular one. A simple model that happens to fit concentrates its mass and wins.
notes.extra: Geometry: Laplace approximation: evidence ≈ best-fit likelihood × (posterior volume / prior volume). The second factor is the Occam penalty: how much of the prior's parameter space had to be thrown away to fit the data.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is a Bayes factor, and what is the Jeffreys-Lindley paradox?
notes.back:
\(BF_{10}=\dfrac{p(x\mid M_1)}{p(x\mid M_0)}\); posterior odds = Bayes factor × prior odds.
Paradox: with a point null and a diffuse prior under the alternative, a result can be "significant" (small p-value) while the Bayes factor strongly favours the null, increasingly so as \(n\to\infty\) or the prior widens.
notes.extra: Geometry: A very wide prior under the alternative wastes almost all its mass on parameter values far from the data, so the alternative predicted the data poorly. Unlike posteriors, Bayes factors never forget the prior; improper priors make them undefined.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: State the Bernstein-von Mises theorem.
notes.back:
Under regularity conditions (fixed finite dimension, prior with positive density at the truth, correct model), the posterior converges to
\(N\!\left(\hat\theta_{MLE},\ I(\theta_0)^{-1}/n\right)\).
The prior washes out, and Bayesian credible sets become asymptotically valid frequentist confidence sets.
notes.extra: Geometry: The log-likelihood paraboloid sharpens at rate n while the log-prior stays fixed: eventually the prior looks flat on the scale of the likelihood peak. Fails when the dimension grows with n, in nonparametric models, at boundaries, and under misspecification (the posterior then has the wrong width: no sandwich correction).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: Posterior mean, median and mode each minimise which expected loss? What is the conceptual weakness of the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate?
notes.back:
Mean: squared error. Median: absolute error. Mode (MAP): 0-1 loss in the limit of a vanishing tolerance window.
MAP is not invariant to reparameterisation: a density transforms with a Jacobian, so the peak moves when you change coordinates. It also ignores posterior mass.
notes.extra: Geometry: A density is "probability per unit volume", and what counts as a unit volume depends on the coordinate system. Mass is real; height is a coordinate artefact. In high dimensions the mode can sit in a region with negligible mass.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is the Jeffreys prior and what is its geometric meaning?
notes.back:
\(p(\theta)\propto\sqrt{\det I(\theta)}\) with \(I\) the Fisher information. It is invariant under reparameterisation.
Examples: Bernoulli gives \(\mathrm{Beta}(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\); Normal scale gives \(p(\sigma)\propto1/\sigma\).
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\sqrt{\det(\text{metric})}\) is the Riemannian volume element. The Jeffreys prior is the uniform distribution on the statistical manifold measured with the Fisher metric: equal prior mass to equal numbers of distinguishable distributions, regardless of how you label them.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is Neal's funnel in hierarchical models and how does the non-centred parameterisation fix it?
notes.back:
With \(\alpha_j\sim N(\mu,\tau)\), when \(\tau\) is small the \(\alpha_j\) are squeezed into a tiny neighbourhood; when \(\tau\) is large they are free. The joint posterior is a funnel whose curvature varies by orders of magnitude; no single sampler step size works, producing divergences.
Non-centred: sample \(z_j\sim N(0,1)\) and set \(\alpha_j=\mu+\tau z_j\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The reparameterisation is a change of coordinates that straightens the funnel into something close to an isotropic blob: the prior dependence between τ and α is moved out of the geometry and into a deterministic transform. Use it when data per group is weak; centred is better when data is strong.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: Describe the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and why it targets the right distribution.
notes.back:
From \(\theta\), propose \(\theta'\sim q(\theta'\mid\theta)\); accept with probability
\(\min\!\left(1,\ \dfrac{p(\theta')\,q(\theta\mid\theta')}{p(\theta)\,q(\theta'\mid\theta)}\right)\), else stay.
Only density ratios are needed, so the normalising constant \(p(x)\) cancels. The rule enforces detailed balance \(p(\theta)T(\theta\to\theta')=p(\theta')T(\theta'\to\theta)\), which makes \(p\) stationary.
notes.extra: Geometry: A hiker who always accepts uphill steps and accepts downhill steps with probability equal to the height ratio. Time spent at each location becomes proportional to height. Random-walk proposals diffuse: distance covered grows only as \(\sqrt{\text{steps}}\), which is hopeless in high dimensions.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is Gibbs sampling, and when does it mix badly?
notes.back:
Cycle through coordinates (or blocks), drawing each from its full conditional \(p(\theta_j\mid\theta_{-j},x)\). A Metropolis-Hastings scheme with acceptance probability 1. Needs tractable conditionals (conjugacy).
Mixes badly when parameters are strongly correlated in the posterior.
notes.extra: Geometry: Moves are axis-aligned. In a narrow diagonal valley each axis-parallel step can only be as long as the valley is wide, so the sampler takes a tiny staircase along the ridge. Fixes: reparameterise/rotate, block correlated parameters, or use gradients.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: How does Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) work, and why does it scale to high dimensions?
notes.back:
Augment \(\theta\) with momentum \(r\sim N(0,M)\). Define the Hamiltonian \(H=-\log p(\theta\mid x)+\tfrac12r^\top M^{-1}r\). Simulate Hamiltonian dynamics with the leapfrog integrator (uses \(\nabla\log p\)), then Metropolis-accept to correct integration error.
Energy is nearly conserved, so distant proposals are accepted with high probability.
notes.extra: Geometry: A frictionless puck on the surface of negative log-posterior, flicked in a random direction. It glides along level sets of energy, following the valley's contours instead of stumbling randomly. Cost to get an independent draw scales like \(d^{5/4}\) versus \(d^2\) for random walk. The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) chooses trajectory length automatically.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is the "typical set" and why does it matter for Bayesian computation?
notes.back:
The region that contains almost all posterior mass. In high dimensions it is a thin shell away from the mode: mass = density × volume, and volume grows explosively with distance from the mode.
Consequences: expectations are determined by the typical set; optimisation (Maximum A Posteriori) finds an atypical point; samplers must explore the shell.
notes.extra: Geometry: For a d-dimensional standard Gaussian the shell sits at radius \(\sqrt d\). The mode is the top of a needle-thin peak: highest, but with essentially no ground around it. A divergent sampler transition signals a region of the shell with curvature too high to be explored.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: Name the key Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) convergence diagnostics.
notes.back:
\(\hat R\) (potential scale reduction): compares between-chain to within-chain variance; want \(<1.01\).
Effective Sample Size (ESS): \(n/(1+2\sum_k\rho_k)\), the number of independent draws equivalent to the autocorrelated chain; check bulk and tail.
Divergences (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo): integrator failed in high-curvature regions, so estimates are biased, not merely noisy.
Also: trace plots, energy diagnostics.
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\hat R\) is a one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) across chains: if chains started in different places still disagree about where the mass is, none of them can be trusted. It can only detect non-convergence, never prove convergence.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What does Variational Inference (VI) optimise? State the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) identity.
notes.back:
Choose \(q\in\mathcal Q\) (tractable family) to minimise \(\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(\theta\mid x))\). Identity:
\(\log p(x) = \underbrace{E_q[\log p(x,\theta)] - E_q[\log q(\theta)]}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(q)} + \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(\theta\mid x))\).
Maximising the ELBO = minimising the KL, without needing \(p(x)\). ELBO = expected log-likelihood − KL(q‖prior).
notes.extra: Geometry: Inference turned into optimisation: project the true posterior onto the manifold of tractable distributions. Fast and scalable, but the answer is biased by the family's shape, typically underestimating variance (mean-field ignores correlations).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: Contrast reverse \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\) with forward \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\) when fitting a unimodal \(q\) to a multimodal \(p\).
notes.back:
Reverse KL(q‖p) (Variational Inference): penalises \(q\) having mass where \(p\) has none. Zero-forcing, mode-seeking: locks onto one mode, too narrow.
Forward KL(p‖q) (maximum likelihood, Expectation Propagation): penalises \(q\) missing mass where \(p\) has some. Mass-covering, moment-matching: straddles all modes, placing mass in the empty valley between them.
notes.extra: Geometry: The expectation is taken under the first argument, and that argument decides where mistakes are noticed. Under q you never look where q is zero, so ignoring a mode is free. Under p you are inspected everywhere p lives, so you must cover it all.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is the Laplace approximation?
notes.back:
Approximate the posterior by a Gaussian centred at the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate with covariance equal to the inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior there:
\(p(\theta\mid x)\approx N(\hat\theta_{MAP},\ H^{-1})\).
Also gives evidence: \(\log p(x)\approx\log p(x,\hat\theta)+\tfrac d2\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log\det H\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Fit the osculating paraboloid to the log-posterior at its peak. Exact when the posterior is Gaussian, good when Bernstein-von Mises has kicked in, poor for skewed, multimodal or boundary posteriors. It is a purely local approximation; it knows nothing beyond the curvature at one point.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is a Gaussian Process (GP), and how does GP regression make predictions?
notes.back:
A distribution over functions such that any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian, specified by mean \(m(x)\) and kernel \(k(x,x')\).
Prediction is Gaussian conditioning: with \(K=k(X,X)\), \(k_*=k(X,x_*)\):
mean \(=k_*^\top(K+\sigma^2I)^{-1}y\), variance \(=k(x_*,x_*)-k_*^\top(K+\sigma^2I)^{-1}k_*\).
Cost \(O(n^3)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: An infinite-dimensional Gaussian ellipsoid over function space, sliced by the hyperplanes "function passes through these data points". The kernel says how strongly nearby function values are tied together; the predictive variance pinches to the noise level at data points and balloons back to the prior far from them.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: How are Bayesian linear regression, ridge regression, kernel ridge regression and Gaussian Process (GP) regression related?
notes.back:
Bayesian linear regression with prior \(\beta\sim N(0,\tau^2I)\): posterior mean = ridge with \(\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2\).
Replace \(x\) by features \(\phi(x)\): the induced kernel is \(k(x,x')=\tau^2\phi(x)^\top\phi(x')\).
GP posterior mean = kernel ridge regression solution. The GP additionally supplies the predictive variance.
notes.extra: Geometry: Weight-space view: a Gaussian blob over coefficient vectors. Function-space view: the same blob pushed through the feature map becomes a Gaussian over functions. The kernel trick lets you work in function space even when the weight space is infinite-dimensional.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is exchangeability and what does de Finetti's theorem say?
notes.back:
A sequence is exchangeable if its joint distribution is invariant under permutation. Weaker than independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.).
de Finetti: an infinite exchangeable sequence is a mixture of i.i.d. sequences:
\(p(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\int\prod_i p(x_i\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta\).
notes.extra: Geometry: If order does not matter to you, you are behaving as if there is an unknown parameter with a prior, and the data are i.i.d. given it. Parameters and priors are not metaphysical assumptions; they are a representation theorem for symmetric beliefs. Also the justification for hierarchical models (exchangeable groups).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is empirical Bayes?
notes.back:
Estimate the prior's hyperparameters from the data by maximising the marginal likelihood \(p(x\mid\eta)=\int p(x\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid\eta)d\theta\), then plug them in and compute posteriors as usual.
A point-estimate approximation to a full hierarchical Bayes model. James-Stein is empirical Bayes for the Normal means problem with the prior variance estimated from \(\|x\|^2\).
notes.extra: Geometry: With many parallel problems (genes, schools, players), the ensemble of noisy estimates reveals the shape of the prior. Each unit then borrows strength from all the others. Understates uncertainty, since hyperparameter uncertainty is ignored.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: How does importance sampling work and why does it break down in high dimensions?
notes.back:
\(E_p[f]=E_q\!\left[f\,\dfrac{p}{q}\right]\approx\dfrac{\sum_i w_if(x_i)}{\sum_i w_i}\), with \(x_i\sim q\), \(w_i=p(x_i)/q(x_i)\).
Needs \(q\) to have heavier tails than \(p\). Effective Sample Size (ESS) \(=(\sum w_i)^2/\sum w_i^2\).
In high dimensions the weight variance grows exponentially in \(d\): one sample carries nearly all the weight.
notes.extra: Geometry: Two thin shells (the typical sets of p and q) in high-dimensional space barely overlap unless p and q are almost identical. Samples from q almost never land where p's mass is.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What are prior predictive and posterior predictive checks?
notes.back:
Prior predictive check: simulate datasets from the prior alone; do they look like plausible data? Catches priors that imply absurd outcomes on the observable scale.
Posterior predictive check: simulate replicated datasets from the fitted model and compare a test quantity \(T(y^{rep})\) with \(T(y)\). Systematic discrepancy reveals misfit.
notes.extra: Geometry: Priors on parameters are hard to judge in parameter space; push them forward into data space, where you have intuition. A posterior predictive check asks whether the observed data would be a typical member of the cloud of datasets the fitted model generates. It uses the data twice, so it is conservative.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::05 Bayesian Statistics
notes.front: What is the Bayes-optimal decision under a loss function?
notes.back:
Choose the action minimising posterior expected loss:
\(a^*=\arg\min_a\int L(\theta,a)\,p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta\).
Inference (the posterior) and decision (the loss) are separated: the same posterior serves any loss. Bayes rules are admissible, and (complete class theorem) essentially every admissible rule is a Bayes rule or a limit of them.
notes.extra: Geometry: The posterior is a map of where the truth might be; the loss says how much each kind of miss hurts. With asymmetric loss (overstocking cheap, stockout costly) the optimal action is a quantile, not the mean.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is Empirical Risk Minimisation (ERM) and what is the generalisation gap?
notes.back:
True risk \(R(f)=E[L(f(x),y)]\); empirical risk \(\hat R(f)=\frac1n\sum_iL(f(x_i),y_i)\). ERM picks \(\hat f=\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal F}\hat R(f)\).
Generalisation gap \(=R(\hat f)-\hat R(\hat f)\), controlled by the capacity of \(\mathcal F\) relative to \(n\).
Excess risk = approximation error (class too small) + estimation error (sample too small) + optimisation error.
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\hat R\) is a noisy copy of the landscape R. Minimising over a big class means searching many places, and somewhere the noise will dip low by chance: the minimiser of a noisy function is biased downward (winner's curse).
