Uniform convergence bounds the worst dip over the class.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension? Give the value for linear classifiers.
notes.back:
The size of the largest point set that the hypothesis class can shatter (realise all \(2^m\) labelings). Hyperplanes in \(\mathbb R^d\) have VC dimension \(d+1\).
Generalisation gap is bounded by roughly \(O\!\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{VC}/n}\right)\). Finite VC dimension is equivalent to (distribution-free) learnability.
notes.extra: Geometry: A line in the plane can shatter 3 points in general position but no set of 4: the XOR labeling of a square's corners cannot be split by a line. Capacity is measured by what labelings you can draw, not by counting parameters: \(\sin(\omega x)\) has one parameter and infinite VC dimension.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is double descent?
notes.back: Test error versus model size follows the classical U-shape up to the interpolation threshold (parameters ≈ samples), where it spikes; beyond it, error falls again, often below the classical minimum.
notes.extra: Geometry: At the threshold exactly one interpolating solution exists and it must contort to fit the noise; its norm explodes (the design matrix is nearly singular). Past the threshold there are infinitely many interpolators and the optimiser picks the minimum-norm one, which gets smoother as more dimensions become available to absorb the noise. Variance peaks at the threshold, then declines. Explicit regularisation flattens the spike.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Why are penalised and constrained forms of regularisation equivalent?
notes.back:
Lagrangian duality: for each \(\lambda\ge0\) there is a \(t\) such that
\(\min_\beta L(\beta)+\lambda\Omega(\beta)\) and \(\min_\beta L(\beta)\ \text{s.t.}\ \Omega(\beta)\le t\)
have the same solution (convex case). Larger \(\lambda\) corresponds to smaller \(t\).
notes.extra: Geometry: At the solution the loss contour is tangent to the constraint boundary: gradients are anti-parallel, \(\nabla L=-\lambda\nabla\Omega\). λ is the exchange rate between the two: how much loss you would save per unit relaxation of the budget.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is the geometry of gradient descent, and how does the condition number control its speed?
notes.back: The gradient is perpendicular to level sets and points in the direction of steepest ascent (in the Euclidean metric). For a quadratic with Hessian eigenvalues between \(\mu\) and \(L\), the best fixed step converges at rate \(\left(\dfrac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\right)\) per step, with \(\kappa=L/\mu\) the condition number.
notes.extra: Geometry: In a round bowl the gradient points at the minimum. In a long narrow valley it points mostly across the valley: the iterate zigzags between the walls and crawls along the floor. The step size is limited by the steepest direction, the progress by the flattest.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: How does Newton's method differ geometrically from gradient descent?
notes.back:
Update \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-H^{-1}\nabla L\). It minimises the local quadratic model exactly, converges quadratically near the optimum, and is invariant to affine reparameterisation.
Cost \(O(d^3)\) per step; can be attracted to saddles in non-convex problems. Quasi-Newton (L-BFGS), Gauss-Newton and natural gradient approximate it.
notes.extra: Geometry: Multiplying by \(H^{-1}\) is a change of coordinates that makes the elliptical valley round, after which the gradient points straight at the minimum. Preconditioning in general = choosing a ruler under which the landscape is isotropic.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What does the noise in Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) do?
notes.back:
Minibatch gradients are unbiased estimates with variance \(\propto1/B\). With a constant learning rate \(\eta\) the iterate does not converge; it hovers in a noise ball of size \(\propto\eta/B\). Decaying \(\eta\) gives convergence.
The noise acts as implicit regularisation: it helps escape sharp minima and saddles and biases toward flat regions. Linear scaling rule: keep \(\eta/B\) roughly constant.
notes.extra: Geometry: A ball rolling on a shaking landscape. It cannot settle in narrow crevices (the shaking bounces it out) but rests happily in wide basins. The effective "temperature" is \(\eta/B\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What do momentum and Adam each add to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)?
notes.back:
Momentum: \(v\leftarrow\beta v+g,\ \theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta v\). Averages gradients over time; improves dependence on condition number from \(\kappa\) to \(\sqrt\kappa\).
Adam: momentum plus per-coordinate scaling by a running root-mean-square of gradients: \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat v}+\epsilon)\). Step size is roughly scale-invariant per parameter.
notes.extra: Geometry: Momentum is a heavy ball: across the valley the zigzag components cancel; along the valley floor they accumulate. Adam is a cheap diagonal preconditioner: it rescales each axis separately to make the valley rounder, but cannot fix valleys that run diagonally.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Define convexity of a function and state why it matters for optimisation.
notes.back:
\(f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\).
Equivalent (differentiable): \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)\); (twice differentiable): Hessian positive semidefinite.
Every local minimum is global; the set of minimisers is convex. Convex losses: least squares, logistic, hinge, with L1/L2 penalties.
notes.extra: Geometry: Chords lie above the graph; tangent planes lie below it. A tangent plane is therefore a global lower bound, so a zero gradient certifies a global minimum. The landscape is a single bowl with no false valleys.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What does a Support Vector Machine (SVM) optimise? What are support vectors?
notes.back:
Hard margin: minimise \(\tfrac12\|w\|^2\) subject to \(y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1\). The margin width is \(2/\|w\|\), so this maximises the margin.
Soft margin = hinge loss \(\max(0,1-y_if(x_i))\) + L2 penalty.
Support vectors are the points on or inside the margin; the solution \(w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_ix_i\) depends only on them.
notes.extra: Geometry: Find the widest street separating the two classes; the boundary is the centre line and the support vectors are the points touching the kerbs. Equivalently, the perpendicular bisector of the shortest segment between the two classes' convex hulls. Remove any non-support point and nothing changes.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is the kernel trick?
notes.back:
Many algorithms use data only through inner products \(x_i^\top x_j\). Replace them by \(k(x_i,x_j)=\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle\) for an implicit, possibly infinite-dimensional feature map \(\phi\), never computing \(\phi\) itself. Valid kernels are the positive semidefinite ones (Mercer).
Radial Basis Function (RBF): \(k=\exp(-\|x-x'\|^2/2\ell^2)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Points inside a circle versus outside are not linearly separable in the plane. Lift with \(\phi(x)=(x_1,x_2,x_1^2+x_2^2)\) onto a paraboloid: a horizontal plane now separates them. A linear method in the lifted space is a nonlinear method in the original space.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: State the representer theorem.
notes.back:
For a regularised problem over a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS),
\(\min_f\sum_iL(y_i,f(x_i))+\lambda\|f\|_{\mathcal H}^2\),
the minimiser has the form \(f^*(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_ik(x_i,x)\).
An infinite-dimensional search reduces to \(n\) coefficients.
notes.extra: Geometry: Decompose any candidate f into a part inside the span of the kernel functions at the data points and a part perpendicular to it. The perpendicular part does not change any fitted value \(f(x_i)\) (reproducing property) but adds to the norm. So it is pure cost: drop it. Same argument as minimum-norm interpolation.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Give three equivalent characterisations of Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
notes.back:
1. Directions of maximum variance: top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.
2. Best rank-\(k\) approximation of the centred data (Eckart-Young): minimises squared perpendicular reconstruction error.
3. The right singular vectors of centred \(X=UDV^\top\); variances are \(d_j^2/(n-1)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Fit an ellipsoid to the data cloud; the principal components are its axes, longest first. Maximising projected variance and minimising perpendicular residual are the same problem by Pythagoras: total squared length = projected + residual, and the total is fixed.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What does the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) \(A=U\Sigma V^\top\) say geometrically?
notes.back:
Every linear map is rotate/reflect (\(V^\top\)), stretch along axes (\(\Sigma\)), rotate/reflect (\(U\)).
The unit sphere maps to an ellipsoid whose semi-axes are \(\sigma_iu_i\). Rank = number of non-zero \(\sigma_i\); condition number \(=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\); truncating gives the best low-rank approximation.
notes.extra: Geometry: \(V\) picks the special orthogonal input directions that remain orthogonal after the map; \(\Sigma\) says by how much each is stretched. The pseudoinverse inverts the stretches it can and zeroes the rest. Near-zero singular values are the source of all ill-conditioning in regression.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Describe k-means: objective, algorithm, geometry, and relation to Gaussian mixtures.
notes.back:
Minimise within-cluster sum of squares \(\sum_i\|x_i-\mu_{c(i)}\|^2\). Lloyd's algorithm alternates (1) assign each point to the nearest centroid, (2) move each centroid to the mean of its points. Each step lowers the objective; converges to a local optimum (use k-means++ initialisation).
It is the hard-assignment, zero-variance limit of Expectation-Maximisation (EM) for a spherical equal-variance Gaussian mixture.
notes.extra: Geometry: Cluster regions are Voronoi cells: convex polytopes bounded by perpendicular bisectors between centroids. So k-means cannot find non-convex, elongated or very unequal-sized clusters.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: In a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) fitted by Expectation-Maximisation (EM), what are the two steps?
notes.back:
E-step: responsibilities \(r_{ik}=\dfrac{\pi_kN(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_j\pi_jN(x_i\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}\).
M-step: responsibility-weighted updates: \(\pi_k=\frac1n\sum_ir_{ik}\), \(\mu_k\) = weighted mean, \(\Sigma_k\) = weighted covariance.
Pitfalls: likelihood unbounded when a component collapses onto a single point; label switching; local optima.
notes.extra: Geometry: Soft Voronoi: each point is shared among ellipsoids in proportion to how well each explains it. Each ellipsoid then re-fits itself to the points it partially owns. Boundaries between components are quadrics rather than flat faces.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What function class does a decision tree represent, and how are splits chosen?
notes.back:
A piecewise-constant function on a partition of feature space into axis-aligned boxes. Splits are chosen greedily to maximise impurity reduction: Gini \(\sum_kp_k(1-p_k)\) or entropy for classification, variance for regression.
Low bias, very high variance; invariant to monotone feature transforms; handles interactions natively.
notes.extra: Geometry: Recursive guillotine cuts of a sheet of paper, each parallel to an axis. A diagonal boundary has to be approximated by a staircase, which is why trees are inefficient for linear structure and unstable to rotations of the features.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Why does bagging reduce variance, and what does the random forest add?
notes.back:
For \(B\) identically distributed predictors with variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\):
\(\mathrm{Var}(\text{average})=\rho\sigma^2+\dfrac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2\).
More trees kill the second term only; \(\rho\sigma^2\) is a floor. Random forests decorrelate trees by restricting each split to a random subset of features, lowering \(\rho\) at a small cost in bias.
notes.extra: Geometry: Vectors of equal length: if they all point the same way, their average is just as long; if they are mutually orthogonal, the average shrinks as \(1/\sqrt B\). Diversity among ensemble members is the resource being exploited.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Explain gradient boosting as optimisation.
notes.back:
Build an additive model \(F_m=F_{m-1}+\nu h_m\). At each stage compute pseudo-residuals \(r_i=-\partial L(y_i,F(x_i))/\partial F(x_i)\) and fit a weak learner \(h_m\) (shallow tree) to them. For squared loss the pseudo-residuals are the ordinary residuals.
Regularisers: shrinkage \(\nu\), subsampling, tree depth, early stopping.
notes.extra: Geometry: Gradient descent in function space. The "parameter vector" is the vector of predictions \((F(x_1),\dots,F(x_n))\); the negative gradient says how each prediction should move; the tree is the closest representable direction to that gradient (a projection onto the weak learner class). Bagging attacks variance; boosting attacks bias.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: k-Nearest Neighbours (kNN): what controls the bias-variance trade-off and why does it suffer in high dimensions?
notes.back:
Predict by majority vote / average of the \(k\) nearest training points. \(k=1\): zero training error, high variance (asymptotic error at most twice the Bayes error). Large \(k\): smooth, high bias.
In high dimensions neighbours are not near: distance concentration makes the "nearest" neighbour almost as far as the farthest.
notes.extra: Geometry: The 1-NN decision regions are the Voronoi tessellation of the training set. Increasing k blurs the tessellation. All distance-based methods are hostage to the choice of metric, so scaling features is part of the model.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: When does a generative Gaussian classifier give a linear boundary? Compare Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) with logistic regression.
notes.back:
Gaussian classes with a shared covariance \(\Sigma\): the log posterior odds are linear in \(x\), with \(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_0)\). Different covariances give a quadratic boundary (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis).
LDA and logistic regression have the same functional form; LDA fits it via the joint density (more efficient if the Gaussian assumption holds), logistic via the conditional likelihood (more robust).
notes.extra: Geometry: Whiten the space with \(\Sigma^{-1/2}\) so both classes become spheres; then classify to the nearest centroid. The boundary is the perpendicular bisector in whitened space, which looks tilted back in the original space.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Why is cross-entropy the standard classification loss, and what does softmax temperature do?
notes.back:
Cross-entropy \(-\sum_ky_k\log p_k\) is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical model: minimising it is maximum likelihood / Kullback-Leibler (KL) minimisation. With softmax \(p_k=e^{z_k/T}/\sum_je^{z_j/T}\) the gradient with respect to the logits is simply \(p-y\).
Temperature \(T\to0\): argmax (one-hot). \(T\to\infty\): uniform.
notes.extra: Geometry: Softmax maps logit space onto the probability simplex; adding a constant to all logits changes nothing (one redundant direction). Temperature scales distance from the simplex centre: low T pushes toward a vertex, high T pulls toward the centroid.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What does the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC) measure, and when should you prefer precision-recall?
notes.back:
The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate over all thresholds. AUC \(=P(\text{score of random positive}>\text{score of random negative})\): a pure ranking measure, invariant to class prevalence and to monotone score transforms.
With heavy class imbalance, prefer precision-recall: precision depends on prevalence and exposes the flood of false positives that a tiny false positive rate hides.
notes.extra: Geometry: Two score histograms (positives, negatives); the threshold is a vertical line sweeping across. ROC traces the two tail areas against each other. AUC measures how little the histograms overlap, and is equivalent to the Mann-Whitney U statistic.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Distinguish calibration from discrimination. What is a proper scoring rule?
notes.back:
Discrimination: ranks positives above negatives (AUC). Calibration: among cases given probability \(p\), a fraction \(p\) are positive. A model can have either without the other.
A proper scoring rule is minimised in expectation by reporting the true probability: log loss, Brier score. Accuracy and AUC are not proper.
Post-hoc fixes: Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling.
notes.extra: Geometry: Reliability diagram: predicted probability versus observed frequency; calibration = hugging the diagonal. Any monotone remapping of scores leaves AUC unchanged but can repair calibration, so the two are orthogonal properties.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is the natural gradient?
notes.back:
\(\tilde\nabla L=F^{-1}\nabla L\), with \(F\) the Fisher information matrix. It is the steepest-descent direction when step length is measured by Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the distributions, not by Euclidean distance between parameters. Invariant to reparameterisation.
Relatives: Fisher scoring, Gauss-Newton, K-FAC, Trust Region Policy Optimisation (TRPO). Adam is a crude diagonal approximation.
notes.extra: Geometry: "Steepest" depends on what counts as a unit step. The Euclidean gradient assumes parameter space is flat with an arbitrary coordinate grid. The natural gradient uses the intrinsic ruler of the statistical manifold, under which equal-length steps change the model's predictions by equal amounts.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is the manifold hypothesis, and what are the cautions when reading t-SNE / UMAP plots?
notes.back:
Real high-dimensional data (images, text, audio) concentrates near a low-dimensional manifold; learning is feasible because the intrinsic dimension, not the ambient one, governs sample complexity.
t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding (t-SNE) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) preserve local neighbourhoods only: cluster sizes, distances between clusters, and apparent density are not meaningful, and results depend on perplexity / neighbour count and seed.
notes.extra: Geometry: A crumpled sheet of paper in 3-D is still 2-D to an ant walking on it. Representation learning un-crumples the sheet so that straight lines in the new coordinates follow the sheet.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: What is data leakage and how does nested cross-validation prevent selection-induced optimism?
notes.back:
Leakage: information unavailable at prediction time (or from the test set) enters training. Typical: preprocessing/feature selection fitted on all data before splitting, duplicates or the same subject across folds, future information in time series, target proxies.
Tuning hyperparameters on the same folds you report makes the score optimistic. Nested CV: inner loop selects, outer loop evaluates the whole selection procedure.
notes.extra: Geometry: The minimum of several noisy estimates is biased low (winner's curse). Everything that looked at the data, including your own choices, is part of the "model" and must sit inside the cross-validation loop.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::06 Machine Learning Core
notes.front: Distinguish covariate shift, label shift and concept drift.
notes.back:
With \(p(x,y)=p(y\mid x)p(x)=p(x\mid y)p(y)\):
Covariate shift: \(p(x)\) changes, \(p(y\mid x)\) fixed. Fix: importance weighting by \(p_{\text{test}}(x)/p_{\text{train}}(x)\).
Label (prior) shift: \(p(y)\) changes, \(p(x\mid y)\) fixed. Fix: re-weight class priors.
Concept drift: \(p(y\mid x)\) itself changes. Fix: new labels, retraining, monitoring.
notes.extra: Geometry: Covariate shift moves the spotlight to a different part of the same function. Harmless for a correctly specified model, harmful for a misspecified one, because the best approximation (the KL projection) depends on where you look.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What function does a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) network compute, geometrically?
notes.back: A composition of affine maps and \(\max(0,\cdot)\): a continuous piecewise-linear function. Each neuron defines a hyperplane; on one side it is off, on the other it is linear. The hyperplanes of all neurons tile input space into convex polytopes, and on each polytope the network is a single affine map.
notes.extra: Geometry: Origami. Each layer folds space along hyperplanes. Depth matters because folds compose: folding an already folded sheet replicates every later cut across all earlier layers. The number of linear regions can grow exponentially with depth but only polynomially with width.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What does the universal approximation theorem say, and what does it not say?
notes.back:
A single hidden layer with enough units and a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to arbitrary accuracy.
It says nothing about: how many units (possibly exponential), whether gradient descent finds the weights, or whether the fit generalises.
notes.extra: Geometry: Sums of shifted ramps or bumps can build any shape, like a Riemann sum or a Fourier series. Existence of a representation is cheap; the questions that matter are efficiency (depth) and learnability.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What is backpropagation?
notes.back:
Reverse-mode automatic differentiation on the computation graph. Forward pass stores activations; backward pass propagates \(\partial L/\partial(\text{node})\) from output to input by the chain rule, as a sequence of vector-Jacobian products.
Cost of the full gradient ≈ 2-3× one forward pass, independent of the number of parameters. Memory scales with depth (stored activations).
notes.extra: Geometry: For a scalar loss, the derivative is a row vector multiplied through a chain of Jacobians. Multiplying from the output side keeps the running quantity a vector; multiplying from the input side would carry full matrices. Reverse mode wins for many inputs to one output; forward mode for one input to many outputs.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: Why do gradients vanish or explode in deep networks, and what are the remedies?
notes.back:
The backpropagated gradient is a product of layer Jacobians. If their singular values are typically \(<1\) the product shrinks exponentially with depth; if \(>1\) it blows up.
Remedies: variance-preserving initialisation, non-saturating activations (ReLU family), residual connections, normalisation layers, gradient clipping, gating (LSTM/GRU).
notes.extra: Geometry: Repeatedly applying a linear map stretches along some directions and squashes along others; after many applications only the extreme directions survive. Stable training needs layer Jacobians that are close to isometries (singular values near 1: "dynamical isometry").

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What is the principle behind Xavier/Glorot and He initialisation?
notes.back:
Choose weight variance so that activation variance (forward) and gradient variance (backward) are preserved across layers.
Xavier: \(\mathrm{Var}(w)=2/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})\) for tanh/linear.
He: \(\mathrm{Var}(w)=2/n_{\text{in}}\) for ReLU (the factor 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the inputs).
notes.extra: Geometry: A sum of \(n\) independent terms has variance \(n\) times that of each term, so weights need variance ∝ 1/n for the pre-activation to stay order one. Makes each random layer approximately length-preserving at the start of training.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What do Batch Normalisation and Layer Normalisation do, and how do they differ?
notes.back:
Both standardise activations to zero mean and unit variance, then apply a learned scale and shift.
BatchNorm: statistics across the batch, per feature; train/inference behaviour differs; weak with small batches.
LayerNorm: statistics across features, per example; batch-independent; standard in Transformers (often as RMSNorm, without centring).
Effect: smoother, better-conditioned loss landscape; larger learning rates.
notes.extra: Geometry: LayerNorm projects each activation vector onto the hyperplane perpendicular to \((1,\dots,1)\) and then onto a sphere of radius \(\sqrt d\): only the direction survives. It also makes the loss invariant to the scale of the preceding weights, so weight norm only affects the effective learning rate.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: How does dropout regularise?
notes.back:
During training each unit is zeroed independently with probability \(p\) (survivors scaled by \(1/(1-p)\)); at test time all units are used.
Interpretations: (1) approximate averaging over an exponential ensemble of weight-sharing subnetworks; (2) multiplicative noise that prevents co-adaptation of features; (3) for linear models, an adaptive L2 penalty. Keeping dropout on at test time gives Monte Carlo uncertainty estimates.
notes.extra: Geometry: Each training step projects the hidden representation onto a random coordinate subspace. A solution that survives all such projections cannot depend on any single coordinate: information must be spread redundantly.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: Why is decoupled weight decay (AdamW) different from L2 regularisation in Adam?
notes.back:
For plain Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) they coincide: \(\theta\leftarrow(1-\eta\lambda)\theta-\eta g\).
In Adam, an L2 term added to the gradient gets divided by \(\sqrt{\hat v}\), so parameters with large gradient history are regularised less. AdamW applies the shrinkage \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\lambda\theta\) outside the adaptive rescaling, giving uniform decay.
notes.extra: Geometry: L2-in-the-loss pulls toward the origin in Adam's warped per-coordinate metric; decoupled decay pulls toward the origin in plain Euclidean space.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: Why do residual connections make very deep networks trainable?
notes.back: A block computes \(x_{l+1}=x_l+f_l(x_l)\). The Jacobian is \(I+\partial f_l/\partial x_l\), so the identity path carries gradients unattenuated across any depth. Blocks only need to learn a correction to the identity, and the network starts close to the identity map.
notes.extra: Geometry: An Euler discretisation of an ordinary differential equation \(\dot x=f(x,t)\): the representation flows through space in small steps rather than being replaced wholesale at each layer. Also behaves like an ensemble of paths of many different lengths. In Transformers the residual stream is a shared communication bus that layers read from and write to.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What inductive biases does a convolutional layer encode?
notes.back: Locality (each output depends on a small neighbourhood), weight sharing (the same filter everywhere), giving translation equivariance: shifting the input shifts the output. Pooling adds approximate translation invariance. Parameter count is independent of image size.
notes.extra: Geometry: Sliding one template across the image and recording the match (inner product) at each location. It is a fully connected layer constrained by symmetry: requiring that the linear map commutes with translations forces it to be a convolution. Generalises to other groups (rotations, permutations giving graph networks).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: Write scaled dot-product attention and explain each geometric ingredient, including the \(\sqrt{d_k}\).
notes.back:
\(\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\).
\(q^\top k\): alignment between a query and each key. Softmax: converts alignments to non-negative weights summing to 1. Output: weighted average of the value vectors.
\(\sqrt{d_k}\): for random unit-variance vectors \(q^\top k\) has variance \(d_k\); without rescaling, softmax saturates and gradients vanish.
notes.extra: Geometry: Each token's output is a convex combination of value vectors, so it lies inside their convex hull: attention interpolates, it cannot extrapolate (the following linear layers and residuals do that). It is a soft, differentiable dictionary lookup; multiple heads look up in several subspaces simultaneously.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: How do learned embeddings represent meaning, and how can a \(d\)-dimensional space hold far more than \(d\) features?
notes.back:
Concepts correspond to directions; similarity is cosine; relations can appear as roughly constant offsets (king − man + woman ≈ queen).
Superposition: in high dimensions one can pack exponentially many nearly orthogonal directions (Johnson-Lindenstrauss). If features are sparse (rarely active together), interference between them is tolerable.
notes.extra: Geometry: Random unit vectors in d dimensions have cosine of order \(1/\sqrt d\): almost everything is almost perpendicular to almost everything else. The price is that individual neurons respond to many unrelated features (polysemanticity).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What does the loss landscape of a large neural network look like?
notes.back: Non-convex, but: critical points with high loss are overwhelmingly saddles, not local minima; local minima tend to have similar, low loss; minima form connected low-loss valleys (mode connectivity). Flat minima tend to generalise better than sharp ones, though flatness is not reparameterisation-invariant.
notes.extra: Geometry: For a critical point to be a minimum, all d Hessian eigenvalues must be positive. If signs were coin flips, that probability is \(2^{-d}\). In a million dimensions there is almost always some direction that leads downhill. Flat minimum: a wide basin, where a small shift between the training and test landscapes changes the loss little.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: Why do heavily overparameterised networks generalise? What is the implicit bias of gradient descent?
notes.back:
Among the infinitely many zero-training-loss solutions, the optimiser selects a particular one. Known cases: linear regression from zero initialisation gives the minimum L2-norm interpolator; logistic regression on separable data converges in direction to the maximum-margin separator.
Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime: infinitely wide networks trained with small learning rate behave as kernel regression with a fixed kernel ("lazy training"); real networks also learn features, which the NTK cannot explain.
notes.extra: Geometry: The set of interpolating solutions is a huge manifold; gradient descent from a small initialisation lands near the point of that manifold closest to where it started. The regulariser is the algorithm and its starting point, not a term in the loss.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: How does a linear autoencoder relate to Principal Component Analysis (PCA)? What does a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) add?
notes.back:
A linear autoencoder with a \(k\)-dimensional bottleneck and squared loss learns the same subspace as the top-\(k\) principal components (not necessarily the same basis).
VAE: probabilistic encoder \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\) and decoder \(p_\theta(x\mid z)\), trained on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) = \(E_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]-\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z))\). The reparameterisation trick \(z=\mu+\sigma\odot\epsilon\) makes sampling differentiable.
notes.extra: Geometry: A nonlinear autoencoder fits a curved k-dimensional manifold instead of a flat subspace. The VAE's KL term forces the codes to fill a standard Gaussian blob without holes, so that every point in latent space decodes to something sensible and you can sample.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What game does a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) play, and what are its failure modes?
notes.back:
\(\min_G\max_D\ E_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)]+E_z[\log(1-D(G(z)))]\).
With an optimal discriminator, the generator minimises the Jensen-Shannon divergence between \(p_{\text{data}}\) and \(p_G\).
Failure modes: mode collapse, oscillation / non-convergence, vanishing generator gradient when \(D\) is too good. Wasserstein GANs replace the divergence by earth-mover distance.
notes.extra: Geometry: Data and generator distributions live on thin low-dimensional manifolds that initially do not overlap; Jensen-Shannon is then constant and gives no gradient. Wasserstein distance measures how far mass must be moved, so it still slopes toward the data.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: How do diffusion models generate data?
notes.back:
Forward process: gradually add Gaussian noise until the data becomes \(N(0,I)\). Reverse process: a network learns to denoise step by step. Training is simple regression: predict the added noise \(\epsilon\) from the noised sample, \(\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2\).
Predicting the noise is equivalent to estimating the score \(\nabla_x\log p_t(x)\) (Tweedie's formula / denoising score matching).
notes.extra: Geometry: The score is a vector field that points uphill in density, toward the data manifold. Noise at many scales blurs the manifold so the field is defined everywhere, even far away. Sampling follows the field from pure noise back to the manifold, with the noise level annealed from coarse to fine.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What does contrastive learning (InfoNCE loss) optimise?
notes.back:
For an anchor, one positive and many negatives:
\(L=-\log\dfrac{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z,z^+)/\tau)}{\sum_j\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z,z_j)/\tau)}\).
A softmax classification of "which candidate is the true positive"; it lower-bounds mutual information between views. Used in SimCLR and CLIP.
notes.extra: Geometry: Embeddings are normalised to the unit hypersphere. The loss decomposes into alignment (pull positive pairs together) and uniformity (spread everything else evenly over the sphere). Temperature τ sets how strongly hard negatives are emphasised.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::07 Deep Learning
notes.front: What do neural scaling laws state, and what was the compute-optimal (Chinchilla) finding?
notes.back:
Test loss falls as a power law in parameters \(N\), data \(D\) and compute \(C\) over many orders of magnitude:
\(L(N,D)\approx E+\dfrac{A}{N^\alpha}+\dfrac{B}{D^\beta}\), with \(E\) the irreducible entropy.
Chinchilla: for a fixed compute budget \(C\approx6ND\), scale \(N\) and \(D\) in equal proportion (about 20 tokens per parameter); earlier large models were undertrained.
notes.extra: Geometry: Straight lines on log-log axes. One proposed origin: the network resolves a data manifold of intrinsic dimension d, and approximation error in d dimensions falls as (number of pieces)\(^{-c/d}\).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Define a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and the Markov property.
notes.back:
A tuple \((\mathcal S,\mathcal A,P,R,\gamma)\): states, actions, transition kernel \(P(s'\mid s,a)\), reward \(R(s,a)\), discount \(\gamma\in[0,1)\). A policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\) maps states to action distributions.
Markov property: the future is conditionally independent of the past given the current state.
notes.extra: Geometry: The state is a sufficient statistic of history for predicting the future. If what you observe is not Markov (one video frame has no velocity), enlarge the state (stack frames, use a recurrent memory, or a belief state).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Define the discounted return. What are the roles of \(\gamma\)?
notes.back:
\(G_t=\sum_{k\ge0}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1}\).
Roles of \(\gamma\): (1) makes infinite-horizon sums finite; (2) sets an effective horizon of about \(1/(1-\gamma)\) steps; (3) equivalent to a per-step termination probability \(1-\gamma\); (4) a bias-variance knob: smaller \(\gamma\) lowers the variance of return estimates at the cost of myopia.
notes.extra: Geometry: An exponentially decaying window over the future. \(\gamma=0.99\) sees about 100 steps ahead, \(\gamma=0.9\) about 10.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Define the state value \(V^\pi\), action value \(Q^\pi\) and advantage \(A^\pi\).
notes.back:
\(V^\pi(s)=E_\pi[G_t\mid s_t=s]\)
\(Q^\pi(s,a)=E_\pi[G_t\mid s_t=s,a_t=a]\)
\(A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)\), with \(E_{a\sim\pi}[A^\pi(s,a)]=0\).
\(V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)Q^\pi(s,a)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: V is the altitude of a state on the landscape of expected future reward. Q is the altitude you would reach by taking a specific first step. Advantage is how much better that step is than your average step from there: it strips out the "this state is just good" component and leaves only what the action contributed.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Write the Bellman expectation equation and its closed-form solution for a finite Markov Decision Process (MDP).
notes.back:
\(V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\left[R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V^\pi(s')\right]\).
In matrix form \(V^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi V^\pi\), so
\(V^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi=\sum_{k\ge0}\gamma^k(P^\pi)^kR^\pi\).
The inverse exists because the spectral radius of \(\gamma P^\pi\) is at most \(\gamma<1\).
notes.extra: Geometry: A self-consistency condition: a state's value = immediate reward + discounted average value of the neighbours it leads to. The Neumann series reads: reward now, plus reward one step out, plus two steps out. Values diffuse backward along the transition graph from where the rewards are.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Why does value iteration converge?
notes.back:
The Bellman optimality operator \((TV)(s)=\max_a\left[R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in the sup norm: \(\|TV-TU\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-U\|_\infty\).
By the Banach fixed-point theorem it has a unique fixed point \(V^*\), and \(\|V_k-V^*\|_\infty\le\gamma^k\|V_0-V^*\|_\infty\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Every application of T shrinks all distances by at least a factor γ, so any two starting guesses are pulled together, and both are pulled to the single point that T leaves fixed. Like repeatedly photocopying at 90%: every image collapses onto the same dot.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Describe policy iteration and state the policy improvement theorem.
notes.back:
Alternate (1) evaluation: compute \(V^\pi\); (2) improvement: \(\pi'(s)=\arg\max_aQ^\pi(s,a)\).
Theorem: if \(Q^\pi(s,\pi'(s))\ge V^\pi(s)\) for all \(s\), then \(V^{\pi'}\ge V^\pi\) everywhere. With finitely many deterministic policies, convergence to \(\pi^*\) is finite, typically in very few iterations.
Generalised policy iteration: any interleaving of partial evaluation and partial improvement; nearly all reinforcement learning algorithms are instances.
notes.extra: Geometry: The set of achievable value functions forms a polytope whose vertices are deterministic policies. Policy iteration hops from vertex to a better vertex, reaching the top corner \(V^*\) that dominates all others. It behaves like Newton's method on the Bellman equation, whereas value iteration is a fixed-point iteration.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Contrast Monte Carlo and Temporal Difference (TD) value estimation.
notes.back:
Monte Carlo: target = full observed return \(G_t\). Unbiased, high variance, needs complete episodes, does not exploit the Markov property.
TD(0): target = \(r+\gamma V(s')\). Bootstraps from the current estimate: biased, low variance, online, exploits Markov structure.
On a fixed batch: Monte Carlo minimises squared error to the observed returns; TD converges to the value function of the maximum-likelihood Markov model of the data.
notes.extra: Geometry: Monte Carlo waits to see how the whole trip turns out. TD updates a guess from a later guess: on your commute, as soon as you hit a traffic jam you revise the arrival estimate without waiting to arrive.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Define the Temporal Difference (TD) error. How do n-step returns and TD(\(\lambda\)) interpolate between TD and Monte Carlo?
notes.back:
\(\delta_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\); update \(V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\delta_t\).
n-step return: \(n\) real rewards then bootstrap. The \(\lambda\)-return is a geometric average of all n-step returns with weights \((1-\lambda)\lambda^{n-1}\): \(\lambda=0\) is TD(0), \(\lambda=1\) is Monte Carlo.
Eligibility traces implement this online: each state keeps a decaying memory, and every TD error updates all recently visited states in proportion.
notes.extra: Geometry: δ is a surprise signal: things went better or worse than expected. It is the reward prediction error that dopamine neurons appear to encode. λ is a slider for how far back in time a surprise assigns credit.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Compare Q-learning and SARSA.
notes.back:
Q-learning (off-policy): \(Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a)+\alpha\left[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-Q(s,a)\right]\). Learns \(Q^*\) regardless of the behaviour policy.
SARSA (on-policy): target \(r+\gamma Q(s',a')\) with \(a'\) the action actually taken. Learns the value of the policy being followed, including its exploration.
notes.extra: Geometry: Cliff-walking: Q-learning learns the optimal path along the cliff edge and keeps falling off during epsilon-greedy exploration; SARSA learns the safer inland path because it prices in its own random missteps. Q-learning evaluates the ideal you, SARSA the actual you.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Name three strategies for the exploration-exploitation trade-off in bandits and their regret.
notes.back:
\(\epsilon\)-greedy: random action with probability \(\epsilon\). Undirected; linear regret for fixed \(\epsilon\).
Upper Confidence Bound (UCB): choose \(\arg\max_a\hat\mu_a+\sqrt{2\ln t/n_a}\): "optimism in the face of uncertainty". Logarithmic regret.
Thompson sampling: sample a model from the posterior, act greedily for it. Logarithmic regret; usually the best in practice.
Lai-Robbins: \(O(\log T)\) regret is the optimal rate.
notes.extra: Geometry: Each arm has an estimate with an error bar. UCB ranks arms by the top of the bar: an arm is tried either because it looks good or because its bar is wide, and trying it shrinks the bar. Thompson sampling picks each arm with exactly the probability that it is the best one.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is the "deadly triad" in reinforcement learning?
notes.back:
Instability or divergence can occur when all three are combined:
1. Function approximation
2. Bootstrapping (Temporal Difference targets)
3. Off-policy training
Any two are safe. Deep Q-Networks (DQN) use all three and rely on stabilisers.
notes.extra: Geometry: The Bellman operator T is a contraction in the sup norm, but applying it takes you out of the subspace of representable value functions; you then project back with Π. Π is a non-expansion in a weighted L2 norm. On-policy, the weighting is the stationary distribution, under which T is also a contraction, so ΠT contracts. Off-policy, the weighting mismatches and the composition ΠT can expand: each step lands further away.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What two tricks stabilise Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and why?
notes.back:
Experience replay: store transitions in a buffer and train on random minibatches. Breaks the temporal correlation of consecutive samples (restores approximately independent data) and reuses experience.
Target network: compute the bootstrap target \(r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_{\theta^-}(s',a')\) with a slowly updated copy \(\theta^-\). Stops the target from moving with every gradient step.
notes.extra: Geometry: Without a target network you are regressing onto a label that shifts whenever you update: a dog chasing its own tail. Freezing the target turns each phase into an ordinary supervised regression problem (fitted Q-iteration).

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is maximisation bias in Q-learning and how does Double Q-learning fix it?
notes.back:
\(E[\max_a\hat Q(s,a)]\ge\max_aE[\hat Q(s,a)]\) (Jensen: max is convex). Using the same noisy estimates both to select and to evaluate the best action yields systematic overestimation, which bootstrapping then propagates.
Double Q-learning: select with one estimator, evaluate with another: \(r+\gamma Q_B(s',\arg\max_{a'}Q_A(s',a'))\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Winner's curse: the highest of several noisy measurements is probably an overestimate, because it was chosen for being high. Re-measure the winner with an independent instrument to get an unbiased reading. Same logic as using held-out data after model selection.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: State the policy gradient theorem. Why is it remarkable?
notes.back:
\(\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=E_{s\sim d^\pi,\,a\sim\pi_\theta}\left[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,Q^\pi(s,a)\right]\).
The gradient does not involve the derivative of the state distribution or of the environment dynamics, so it can be estimated from sampled trajectories of an unknown, non-differentiable environment. REINFORCE uses the sampled return \(G_t\) in place of \(Q^\pi\).
notes.extra: Geometry: The score-function (log-derivative) trick: \( abla E_p[f]=E_p[f abla\log p]\). \( abla\log\pi(a\mid s)\) is the direction in parameter space that makes action a more probable; weight it by how good the action turned out. "Do more of what worked, less of what did not", with the environment as a black box.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Why does subtracting a baseline in policy gradients leave the gradient unbiased while reducing variance?
notes.back:
For any \(b(s)\) not depending on the action:
\(E_{a\sim\pi}[ abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a\mid s)\,b(s)]=b(s) abla_ heta\sum_a\pi_ heta(a\mid s)=b(s) abla_ heta1=0\).
So \(Q^\pi\) may be replaced by \(Q^\pi-b\). Choosing \(b=V^\pi\) gives the advantage and large variance reduction.
notes.extra: Geometry: The expected score is zero, so the baseline is a control variate: a zero-mean term correlated with the noise. If every reward is around +100, raw REINFORCE pushes up every sampled action and relies on tiny differences; centring asks the right question: better or worse than average?

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is an actor-critic method, and what does Generalised Advantage Estimation (GAE) do?
notes.back:
Actor: the policy \(\pi_\theta\), updated by policy gradient. Critic: a learned \(V_\phi\) that supplies low-variance advantage estimates in place of Monte Carlo returns.
GAE: \(\hat A_t=\sum_{l\ge0}(\gamma\lambda)^l\delta_{t+l}\), an exponentially weighted sum of Temporal Difference (TD) errors. \(\lambda=0\): one-step TD (low variance, biased by critic error); \(\lambda=1\): Monte Carlo (unbiased, high variance).
notes.extra: Geometry: Generalised policy iteration with function approximators: the critic is approximate policy evaluation, the actor approximate policy improvement. λ dials how much you trust the critic versus the actual observed rewards.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What problem do trust-region methods (TRPO, PPO) solve, and how?
notes.back:
A policy-gradient step that is too large collapses performance, and the data was collected under the old policy, so it cannot reveal this. Equal steps in parameter space can mean wildly unequal changes in behaviour.
Trust Region Policy Optimisation (TRPO): maximise the surrogate \(E\!\left[\dfrac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{old}}}\hat A\right]\) subject to \(\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\text{old}}\|\pi_\theta)\le\delta\) (a natural-gradient step).
Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO): clip the ratio to \([1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]\) so there is no incentive to move far.
notes.extra: Geometry: Measure step size in distribution space (a KL ball around the current policy), not in parameter space. The surrogate objective is only a trustworthy local map near the old policy; the trust region is the area where the map is still accurate.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: On-policy versus off-policy learning: definitions and the role of importance sampling.
notes.back:
On-policy: learn about the policy that generated the data (SARSA, PPO). Stable, sample-hungry.
Off-policy: learn about a target policy \(\pi\) from data generated by a behaviour policy \(\mu\) (Q-learning, DQN, SAC). Enables replay buffers and learning from logs.
Correction by importance ratios \(\prod_t\pi(a_t\mid s_t)/\mu(a_t\mid s_t)\): unbiased, but the variance grows exponentially with the horizon. Remedies: truncated ratios (Retrace, V-trace), per-decision weighting.
notes.extra: Geometry: A product of many ratios is a random walk in log space; after T steps a few trajectories carry all the weight. One-step Q-learning avoids the ratios because its target conditions on the action and takes the max itself.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What are the promise and the central difficulty of model-based reinforcement learning?
notes.back:
Learn \(\hat P,\hat R\), then plan: Dyna (augment real data with simulated rollouts), Model Predictive Control (MPC), Monte Carlo Tree Search (AlphaZero, MuZero). Far more sample-efficient.
Difficulty: compounding model error: one-step errors accumulate over a rollout, and the planner actively exploits model inaccuracies, steering toward regions where the model is optimistically wrong.
Mitigations: short rollouts, model ensembles with uncertainty penalties, replanning each step, value-equivalent latent models.
notes.extra: Geometry: A map versus walking the territory. Planning on the map is free, but errors grow with route length, and an optimiser searching the map for shortcuts will find exactly the places where the cartographer made a mistake.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and how is it reduced to an MDP?
notes.back:
The agent receives observations \(o\sim O(\cdot\mid s)\), not states. The belief state \(b(s)=P(s\mid\text{history})\), updated by Bayes filtering, is a sufficient statistic for the history, and the belief-state process is a (continuous-state) MDP.
The optimal finite-horizon value function over beliefs is piecewise linear and convex. Exact solution is intractable; practice uses recurrent policies or frame stacking.
notes.extra: Geometry: The belief is a point in the probability simplex over states. Value = upper envelope of hyperplanes (one per conditional plan). Convexity means certainty is valuable: corners of the simplex are worth more than the centre, which is why information-gathering actions can be optimal despite yielding no reward.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: Which reward transformations preserve the optimal policy? What is reward hacking?
notes.back:
Potential-based shaping \(F(s,a,s')=\gamma\Phi(s')-\Phi(s)\) preserves optimal policies for any potential \(\Phi\) (Ng, Harada, Russell 1999), and is essentially the only additive form that does so. A good choice is \(\Phi\approx V^*\).
Reward hacking (specification gaming): the agent maximises the literal reward in unintended ways (Goodhart's law).
notes.extra: Geometry: Shaping terms telescope along any trajectory: the total added reward depends only on the endpoints, like a conservative force field. It reshapes the hills to make them easier to climb without moving the summit. Any non-conservative bonus creates cycles the agent can farm forever.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is maximum-entropy reinforcement learning (Soft Actor-Critic, soft Q-learning)?
notes.back:
Objective: \(J(\pi)=E\left[\sum_t r_t+\alpha\,\mathcal H(\pi(\cdot\mid s_t))\right]\).
Optimal policy is a Boltzmann distribution \(\pi^*(a\mid s)\propto\exp(Q_{\text{soft}}(s,a)/\alpha)\), and the hard max in the Bellman backup becomes a log-sum-exp (soft max).
Benefits: principled exploration, robustness, keeps multiple good behaviours alive.
notes.extra: Geometry: "Control as inference": condition a graphical model on optimality and the posterior over trajectories is this policy; it is Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularised reinforcement learning toward a uniform prior. The temperature α melts the argmax vertex of the simplex into a smooth interior point; α → 0 recovers standard reinforcement learning.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is the core difficulty of offline (batch) reinforcement learning?
notes.back:
Learning from a fixed dataset without further interaction. The backup \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) queries actions never seen in the data; their Q-values are unconstrained extrapolations, the max selects the most overestimated ones, bootstrapping propagates the error, and no new data ever corrects it.
Remedies: keep the policy near the behaviour policy (behaviour-cloning regularisation, BCQ), pessimism (Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) pushes Q down on unseen actions), uncertainty penalties.
notes.extra: Geometry: The data covers only a thin tube of state-action space. Outside the tube the Q-function is unconstrained fantasy, and an optimiser is drawn to fantasy. Offline reinforcement learning is constrained optimisation: improve as much as possible while staying inside the tube.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: How does Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) work, and how does Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplify it?
notes.back:
1. Collect pairwise preferences; fit a reward model under Bradley-Terry: \(P(y_w\succ y_l)=\sigma(r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l))\).
2. Optimise the policy: \(\max_\pi E[r(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}})\), typically with Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO).
The KL-regularised optimum has closed form \(\pi^*\propto\pi_{\text{ref}}\exp(r/\beta)\). DPO inverts this, \(r=\beta\log(\pi/\pi_{\text{ref}})+\text{const}\), substitutes into the Bradley-Terry likelihood, and trains the policy directly with a logistic loss: no reward model, no sampling loop.
notes.extra: Geometry: The KL term is a leash to the reference model: the learned reward is only trustworthy near the data it was trained on, and an unleashed optimiser would find its blind spots (reward hacking). Same trust-region logic as TRPO and offline reinforcement learning.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is the occupancy-measure (linear programming) view of a Markov Decision Process (MDP)?
notes.back:
Define the discounted occupancy \(\rho^\pi(s,a)=\sum_t\gamma^tP(s_t=s,a_t=a)\). Then \(J(\pi)=\sum_{s,a}\rho^\pi(s,a)R(s,a)\) is linear in \(\rho\). The valid occupancies are those satisfying linear flow-conservation constraints
\(\sum_a\rho(s',a)=\mu_0(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}P(s'\mid s,a)\rho(s,a)\),
a convex polytope. Solving the MDP is a linear programme; its dual variables are the values \(V(s)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: A linear objective over a polytope is maximised at a vertex, and vertices correspond to deterministic policies: this is why an optimal deterministic policy always exists. Reward is a direction in occupancy space; the optimal policy is the corner of the polytope furthest along it. \(J\) is non-convex in policy parameters, but linear in the right coordinates.

notes.deck: Statistics, Bayes, ML & RL (geometric)::08 Reinforcement Learning
notes.front: What is the credit assignment problem, and which mechanisms address it?
notes.back:
Determining which earlier actions were responsible for a delayed outcome. With sparse, delayed reward the learning signal per decision is tiny and noisy.
Mechanisms: value functions (turn delayed reward into immediate Temporal Difference errors), eligibility traces / n-step returns, advantage baselines (remove what was not the action's doing), discounting (assume nearer actions matter more), reward shaping, hindsight relabelling, hierarchy / options.
notes.extra: Geometry: A value function is a potential field over states that turns a distant goal into a local slope. Once V is accurate, acting well is just climbing the local gradient, and the long-horizon problem has been compiled into a one-step one.
